speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice):
speechtext:
I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe):
That the said1 Bill be not now read the third time, but be referred back to the Committee of the Whole, with power to amend same by substituting the following for section 3'0.
30. Subject to the provisions of section three of this Act, power to remove or dismiss any deputy head, officer, clerk or employee, shall vest in the Commission.
Before exercising such power, the Commission shall require a statement in writing, from the minister in the case of a deputy head, and from the deputy head in all other cases, giving! the causes, reasons and facts invoked for such dismissal.	. .
Upon receipt of such statement in writing the Commission shall forthwith communicate a copy of same to the deputy head or other employee whose dismissal is sought.	_
The deputy head or employee shall within ten days after the receipt of copy of said statement file with the Commission a statement in writing in answer to such charges in default of which the Commission may proceed on the statement submitted asking for dismissal.
I do not want to make any further remarks on this amendment except this: When the Bill was before the House, it provided that the power of dismissal should be vested in the Governor in Council, hut no power of appointment was provided in the Bill. The only section that had any reference as to Low employees should come into the service was the one providing that, on the request of a deputy head, the commission should, as it saw fit, in its best judgment, supply the proper person. We had the Bill amended to vest the power of appointment in the commission by substituting the word " appoint " for the word " supply." Consequently the amendment which I have just moved should be passed so as to make section 30 conform with the rest of the Bill. When I moved that
amendment the first time I explained my reasons for it. I then stated that it was only fair that the body which had the power of appointment should also, have the power of dismissal, and. I wanted this amendment to carry for another reason. My contention is that even if the power of dismissal rests in the Governor in Council, any one whose dismissal is asked for should have an opportunity of stating his case and submitting his answer to the power which is to dismiss him. My amendment is-, I think, just and fair, and the Civil Service employee is entitled to a certain amount of protection by being allowed, whenever charges are made against him or whenever his dismissal is asked, at least to submit his case. It was argued in answer that this might involve a good deal of work on the part of the commission. Certainly we cannot expect that there will be a trial each time a dismissal- is requested, .but the least this House should do is to give the employee, who is charged with any offence or whose dismissal is requested, the privilege of putting his reason in writing and having them made part of the record of his dismissal.

The amendment proposed by my hon. friend was very thoroughly discussed when the Bill was being considered in committee, and there is nothing that I can add to what I said at that time. The intent of the Civil Service Act is to provide a different method so far as the appointment of civil servants is concerned. It was not intended that we should change the existing method of dismissing officials.
The purport of the Bill was to abolish patronage.
Patronage in the matter of appointing officials.
Not in the matter of dismissals?

My hon. friend contends that the Civil Service Commission have the power of dismissing even deputy ministers and deputy heads, and I submit that is not a fair proposition and should not receive the support of the House.
On the recommendation of the minister?

On the recommendation of anybody. I wish to repeat what I have already said on more than one occasion in this House, namely, that civu servants are employees of the Crown. They

are paid by the Crown, and the power of dismissal should rest in the Crown and in no other body, the Crown being responsible to Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, 'before the motion for the third reading of this Bill is carried, I desire to repeat what I said in committee that this Bill, instead of abolishing patronage, affords a greater incentive to the exercise of patronage than has existed in this country since 1908. I will prove that by a very brief reference to the old statute and to the Bill in its present form. The Act of 1908, section 42, provided that:
No person shall, directly or indirectly, solicit or endeavour to influence any minister of the Crown or the head of any department with respect to the appointment of any person to the service, or with respect to the promotion or transfer of or an increase of salary to, any officer, clerk, or employee in the public service.
(2) Any person who, directly or indirectly, solicits or endeavours to influence any minister of the Crown or the head of any department in favour of his appointment or promo-

tion or to increase his salary, shall he deemed to be unworthy of such appointment, promotion or increase, and it shall not be accorded him ; and if he is employed in the public service he shall be liable to immediate dismissal.
When the Bill, whose third reading has now been moved, was drafted, the efficacy of that section was .recognized because it was repeated in the Bill as section 9 and a third ! subsection was added in these terms:
Any person shall have the right to submit to the Commission a representation in writing with respect to the appointment of any person to the public service or with respect to the promotion, transfer of or an increase of salary to any officer, clerk or employee in the public service.

Suppose an officer
of a department wanted to be promoted and placed1 a statement before the commission, would he contravene the Act?

Not under this. The
question the ex-IMinister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) asks reminds me that when this matter was under discussion a few days ago the .right hon. the Prime Minister pointed out that the remedy of the official would be the very one suggested, by my hon. friend.
Perfectly proper.

Perfectly proper, as my
hon. friend says, and yet this section, as it has existed since 1908 with this new subsection, was stricken out of this Act at the demand of an hon. gentleman supporting the Government and representing one of the Toronto seats. So that, this Act, not only does not preserve the safeguard against patronage	that the
old Act contained but	it throws
the door wide open to the exercise of patronage. I am of opinion, Mr. Speaker, that had the right hon. the Prime Minister been in the House at the time the demand came from the Government side of the House for the elimination of that section, my right hon. friend would never have acceded to it. However, that demand has been acceded to and the new Act shorn of that protection, coupled with the fact that 15,000 or 20,000 employees of the Outside Service are still left outside of the operation of the Act, and coupled with the dual complexion of the support of this Government, convinces me that this Act not only does not abolish patronage, but that patronage under it will be more rampant than ever. From what I have heard, I am certain that a well known medical principle will he applied in the operation of this Act. It is that when a
person takes poison an antidote is administered. I am satisfied that the principle that will be applied in the operation of this Act in future will be that when a Grit gets an- appointment a Tory will have to get another to wipe out the effect of the first.

Has the Internal Economy Commission of the House made any report to Parliament this year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Speaker is a member of the Commission ^of Internal Economy of the House, and ,in that capacity he has (been making the inquiry alluded to by the hon, member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson). The report has not been brought to my attention yet-in fact, I do not know whether it is completedt-tout I have understood from H's Honour the Speaker that he expects to effect very considerable economies in the affairs of the House toy the new dispositions which he will propose.	[DOT]
So far as the observations of my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) aTe concerned, I cannot concur in the view which he has taken. It seems to me a singularly exaggerated view. The subsection which he condemns, as far as I understand his argument, is this:
Any person shall have the right to submit to the Commission a representation in writing with respect to the appointment of any person to the public service or with respect to the promotion, transfer of or an increase of salary to any officers, clerk or employee in the public service.
The purpose of that section, as I understand, is to give reasonable opportunity to men employed in the public service to make their representations, in an open and proper way, to the Civil Service Commission. It seemed undesirable that they should be absolutely cut off from a representation either tO' the minister to whose department [DOT]they belong, or to the Civil Service Commission itself. How this would lead to the increase of patronage in the ordinary sense is entirely beyond my comprehension. The exercise of patronage in the past, as it has been condemned on both sides of the House, is the exercise by ministers of the Crowm of the power of appointment, not in the public interest, as it is said, but in a party interest. The Civil Service Comnrs-sion is an absolutely independent body,

which is bound to make appointments to the public service upon competitive examination, or for reasons which are absolutely in the public interest. To suggest, therefore, that the giving of this right to public servants to make their representations in written form and in an open manner to the Civil Service Commission will lead to the continuance, or the increase, of patronage, seems to me to be absolutely beyond the bounds of common sense.
With regard to the Bill as a whole, hon. gentlemen will realize that it necessarily has been prepared under very great stress, and possibly without the opportunity of giving to it the prolonged consideration which ought to be given to a
12 n. very important Bill of this character. It brings under the control of the Civil Service Commission many thousands of employees throughout the country: I am informed by the Acting Minister of Finance, who has had charge of "the Bill, that the number will not fall short of fifty-five thousand. To undertake that the appointments of so large a number of public servants shall be made under the direction of the Civil Service Commission is obviously a very great step in advance, and I should not be at all surprised if it were found necessary at the next session of Parliament to go over this Bill again, to improve it if possible, and to amend it in the light of the experience which will have been gained in its practical operation during the next six or seven months. There is a desire, I believe, on both sides of the House to make the Bill as effective and as workable as possible. We shall endeavour to join our efforts for that purpose at the next session, in so far as it may be found necessary by reason of the experience which will have been gained by the Civil Service Commission in the meantime.
A reference has also been made in the House to the importance of having the commission strengthened in personnel by an increase of members.
And in salary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And in salary also, my hon. friend suggests. Well, those are matters which must be taken into consideration in the meantime. Obviously the extension of the scope of the Commission to fifty-five thousand public servants will entail upon the members of the Commission an enormously increased responsibility and very great additional labour. How those labours can best be discharged

we shall have to consider between now and the next session, if it turns out in the meantime that the Commission as at present constituted is not able to give to all these matters the direct personal attention which will obviously be necessary. In the past when discussing the question of Civil Service reform, and how it would be possible to deal with fifty or sixty thousand additional public servants by means of the Civil Service Commission, the suggestion has been made to me that possibly local boards might have to be established in each province in Canada for the purpose of reporting directly to a central board here. That would be one method. Another method, which has been suggested to the House, is the increase of the personnel of the Board by one or two members. However, the subject will be open at the next session of Parliament.
I need only add this further observation :	Reference has been made to the
desirability of having returned soldiers represented on the 'Commission. If it becomes necessary to increase the personnel of the Commission, I think hon. members may rest assured that the claims of returned soldiers will not be overlooked or forgotten. It is quite proper that they should be considered, and furthermore, that action should be taken upon that consideration. But I know the spirit of the returned men too well to believe that they would desire the personnel of the Civil Service increased un'ess it were in the public interest to do so. It may, and very probably it will, become necessary in the public interest to make some increase, and hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this subject along that line may rest assured that this matter -which has been under consideration before it was brought up in the House-together with any suggestions which they have made in that connection, will not be overlooked.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysboro):
speechtext:
To my mind the great defect in this proposal is the fact that the railway employees have not been included, and there is no branch of the service in Eastern Canada that has been used for patronage purposes as have the Government railways. The Government are retaining the right to continue the old system, which is wrong and out-of-date, as every one admits; not only on the Intercolonial but all the Government railways. We were told the other day that the Intercolonial employs some twenty thousand men. And when the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern are taken in, the number of employees will be increased perhaps to hundreds of thousands. It is of the greatest importance that this question should be considered at this stage. I have not heard any good reason given by any member of the Government why the railways should not be included. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Maclean) said in a former speech that instructions had been given to the management of the Intercolonial railway to discontinue the patronage system. , He was asked to produce the instructions and to lay them on the Table, and he was not able to do so. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) himself, was pressed for a clear statement on that question the other night, and he admitted that he did not send out any instructions, that he had had a conversation with the general superintendent of the Intercolonial, in which he had told him that he had a free hand to abolish patronage if he wished to do so. That is no way to abolish patronage. Something more definite than that must be done. Instructions must be sent out. The system has existed so long that it has permeated the whole of Eastern Canada, and patronage will never be abolished merely by having a conversation with an official of the Intercolonial

The Government must announce to every superintendent and every foreman in the workshops along the line that they are to have a free hand to employ the men required. Why should a boy, who wants to be an engineer or a driver on the road, or to start in as a brakeman and grow up to be a conductor, have to go to a member of Parliament or -to a patronage committee before he can be taken on? That is the present system. No young boy can get into the shops unless he is armed with a certificate from a member of Parliament or a patronage committee. That system exists in Nova Scotia, notwithstanding the declaration of the Prime Minister, and it is still as rampant as ever it was. And it is only a pretense to say that there was a conversation with the general superintendent of the road. If such instruction was given, it has never reached the superintendents or the men along the line who are foremen in the shops and who employ the men. If the Government is sincere about this they must do something more than they have done in the past. It is idle to say that we are abolishing patronage throughout Canada if we still continue it on the Government railways.

I was very much pleased indeed to hear the Premier's promise that if it is necessary to enlarge the Civil Service Commission a returned soldier will be placed on it. I may say that I would have been better pleased if one had been placed there already. I think it is absolutely necessary, as the hon. member for Fort William has said, that if we are going to do justice to the soldier, we should bring that justice into the realm of practical politics. Personally, it is very disagreeable to me, and to every boy who has served overseas, to have so much notoriety given in this House and in the newspapers to the returned soldiers. When a man in this House wants to draw applause he simply has to refer to something which has been done on the western front by *the Canadians. I think we are all more interested in the future of the returned men than we are in the applause of this House; and I would like to see this matter brought into the realm of practical politics, where something can be done in a practical way to place these men in the public service. I do not see any way by which it can so easily and so well be accomplished than by having a representative on the commission. I am not pleading that the returned men should get any preference if they are not capable, for that

would be fatal to their best interests, But other things being equal, I think they should have the preference. And if we are going to give 'them a preference, we should start about it in a practical way.

I do not wish to repeat the arguments set forth by the hon. member for Russell with regard to the disappearence from the Bill of section 9. But I wish to endorse everything he has said in that connection. I consider that section 9 was by far the most important section of the Bill, so far as doing away with patronage and political influence is concerned. I desire accordingly to move, seconded by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie):
That this Bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House to restore Section 9 of the Bill as at first submitted! to the House.

Mr. Speaker, when we were in
committee on this Bill, section 9 was discussed and the opinion of the committee was that it was not advisable to have that section embodied in the Bill. The reasons for coming to that conclusion were advanced at that time, and, to my mind at least, they were sufficient to justify the leaving out of that section. I have listened to the arguments advanced with regard to the amendment which has just been voted down; and I have listened to the statement made by the Prime Minister with regard to what might possibly be done at the next session of Parliament if defects were found in the present Bill, which possibly was drafted' rather hurriedly owing to the amount of work that has been before the Government.
Upwards of a year ago instructions were sent out that only those who had seen service at the front should be considered in the matter of appointments to the Civil Service both the Inside and the Outside service, where such men could be had, and I believe that that course was observed by those sending in recommendations to the Government from that time on. I cannot help but feel, in view of the fact that a Committee on Pensions is now sitting in this House, that this matter should1 have received some attention at the hands of the Government as well as at the hands of the representatives in Parliament. I do think that the soldiers would have felt that their interests were being safeguarded and looked after much better had a returned soldier been ap-

pointed as one of the members of this commission.
Under ithe proposal to reinsert this clause in the Bill, we are justified in considering the present personnel of the commission. It is not a pleasant thing to do, particularly when one happens to he acquainted with these gentlemen and to have a personal high regard for them. But in the selection of the members of the Civil Service Commission I do not believe that care has been taken to obtain men of outstanding administrative ability such as is necessary for the exercising of such tremendous power, influence and responsibility as will devolve upon this body. More than 55,000 men in the public service will be placed directly under the control of this commission. I submit that among returned soldiers men could have been found possessing the qualifications which I have mentioned; yet, for some reason, no returned soldier has been selected to fill one of these positions. The greatest problem of this country to-day is how to look after the men who are returning from the front. This problem will be before us for years, and I do not think that next session is the proper time to consider the matter, nor do I think that a com mission of three is sufficient to look after it at this time. It has been intimated that local boards may have to be established throughout the country in order to facilitate the work of the commission. Under the clause which is proposed to be reinserted it would almost appear necessary that the members of this commission should be arrayed in uniform, or ito have some distinguishing mark to indicate that they are the Civil Service Commission, and that it is not advisable for any representative of the people to go within speaking distance of them; otherwise it may be implied that somebody's interest is to be advanced or jeopardized. These men have ordinary human instincts; they have their social connections, and if a provision of this kind is inserted in the Bill many deserving applicants will be placed at a disadvantage . and the cases of others will be advanced because of their social connection with the members of this commission. The representatives of the people should not be deprived of all responsibility in matters of this kind.. Judging from my experience in the county from which I come, I do not believe that abuses have arisen in connection with appointments. When the subject was being discussed on the hustings members of the present Government referred more particularly to the expenditure of money involved under the patronage
system than to the advisability of having all appointments made by the Civil Service Commission. In one of the first meetings held in Winnipeg the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. T. A. Crerar) said, as reported in the Manitoba Free Press, that he had already been approached by some one who wanted to dispose of a patent for certain purposes and by some one from Ontario who wished him to use his influence respecting an appointment to the Upper House. These were the things uppermost in his mind, apparently, when he wa6 referring to patronage. Yet under no measure that has been introduced are the Government being freed from, this patronage so condemned by them at that time. Under this provision the representatives of the people will not dare place before the Civil Service Commission their views respecting the qualifications of any candidate or applicant for a position, in the Civil Service.
I do not think it is possible to make a more severe reflection on the representatives of the people than is embodied in the clause which it is now proposed to reinsert in the Bill. I do not believe that it was in the public interest to introduce a Bill of this - kind. You are creating a class corporation in this country. You are erecting a wall of protection around them. You are placing the most absolute power in the hands of this commission, and, under this clause, you seek to deprive the representatives of the people of the right to go. near this body, upon whom you have conferred such vast powers, for an applicant to advance his or her claims for consideration. I do. not think it is in the public interest that this clause should be reinserted in the Bill.

With some of the .features of this Bill I do not agree, but a body of opinion throughout the country is in favour of some such measure as this. Never having had great reverence for the doctrine of infallibility, however, I shall allow my judgment to give way to. what I believe -to be the judgment of the vast majority of the people and of most of the members of this House. No great harm can be done in. the next six or eight months by allowing this Bill to go through now. I am satisfied that next session it will come up for reconsideration and, with our larger experience, we shall probably be able to improve it.
But I rise principally to endorse the remarks, made by the members for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), and Muskoka (Mr. Peter McGibbon), who supported the suggestion that a returned

soldier should toe appointed to the Civil Service Commission. I think that should be done now. We have to consider the cost of all these things; it is right that we should be economical. But I will tell the Government where they can get the money to pay the salary of this returned soldier for at least a year as a member of this commission. They have only to make a certain gentleman whose name I dare not mention here refund $5,000 that he looted from the Treasury and that he did not earn. That will pay the salary of this returned soldier on the board for one year, and next year we may consider where we can get the salary for the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the amendment were that no person should approach the Civil Service Commission in the way indicated, I should be rather inclined to vote for the re-insertion of the clause, but the clause, as it appeared in the original Bill, was that no person should approach a minister of the Crown. I must say that, on careful consideration, that looks like an interference with responsible Government. Almost anybody should have the right in a respectful way to approach any minister of the Crown on any matter of public business. If, however, it were deemed necessary to move an amendment to insert a section that no person should approach the Civil Service Commission in that way, I am inclined to think I would support it, because the Civil Service Commission is supposed to be a judicial commission, and we would not, for one moment, tolerate the idea of any person approaching the judges of the land in order to exercise undue influence. But as respects the right to approach a minister of the Crown and discuss any matter with him and even to ask or advise him respecting appointments to any public office, I should not like to interfere with that right or privilege, although apparently that has been done in the past. I know that section has not been respected in the past, and I do not think it would be respected in the future.

The hon. member for Kamouraska -((Mr. E. Lapointe) is quite within his right, but nevertheless I am sorry he is going to divide the House upon this matter. Personally I would have preferred that this section ha-d been left in the Bill. I withdrew it because that seemed to be the unanimous opinion of the House at the time. I do not recollect any single person suggesting that the section should remain in the Bill. I think sometime afterwards the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) expressed his regrets that the section was dropped.
I objected at the time.

Had I not been left with the impression that it was the unanimous view of the House that any person should have the right of approaching ministers of the Cr-own, I should not -have dropped the section, and T regret the hon. member -for Kamouraska is going to inconvenience the House by dividing it on this matter.
I made my view at the time as plain as words could make it.

I am sorry I was
not in the House at the time.

Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to say that I am not in full sympathy with this Bill, although I do not purpose voting .against it. I believe it will do no harm to try it out for at least six or eight months, and then, if necessary, it may be amended. But I feel that the Bill, as it at present exists, will not greatly improve conditions in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to give expression to my unqualified support of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr Fielding). If there is anything this House ought to do, it is to make the Civil Service Commission absolutely independent of every outside influence, to surround it with all the safeguards vouchsafed to the judiciary of this country. It should not be permitted to be approached by any other than, at any rate, the ministers. T hope, therefore, my hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe) will amend his motion so as to make it conform with the suggestion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens.
The salaries of the commissioners are not high enough. Instead of having $5,000 a year, they should have $7,000. You cannot expect judicial service unless you pay a man a proper salary. The commissioners should receive the salary of a Supreme Court judge, and they should: have all the sanctity that can be given to a commission that is absolutely judicial in its capacity.

I desire to endorse the remarks of my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) with reference to withdrawing the employees of the Intercolonial and other Government railways from the operation of this Bill.
At one o'clock the House rose.
The House resumed at three o'clock.

When we separated at' one
o'clock I had just risen to express my very great regret that the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean), who is piloting this Bill through the House, was unable to persuade his colleagues to bring
135i
the employees of the Government railway system under the operation of the Civil Service Act the same as those of other departments. 1 am sure that any one who has any knowledge or experience of the great evil of patronage that seems to be in the mind of every hon. member of this House, must realize that if there is one department more than another in which it is present, in the greatest possible degree, it is that of the Government railway system. If, in order to abolish patronage the Civil Service Commission is to take practically complete control of the appointment and promotion of civil servants, I cannot understand why the employees of the Government railway system should not also come under the direction of the commission. The hon. the Acting (Minister of Finance, during the past two or three years, took very .strong ground against the evils of patronage and demanded that they should be abolished. The hon. gentleman's own constituency, and the Maritime Provinces generally, must be more affected by the Intercolonial than other parts of the Dominion and therefore, my hon. friend being a representative of that part of the country, has complete knowledge of the great disadvantages arising from the existence of the patronage system as applied . to the Intercolonial.	.
Personally, I have very little confidence that the Bill will have any great effect in doing away with the patronage evil. But it will be of some use to the ministers because they will be able to employ it as a sort of buffer between themselves and the applicants when they desire to do so and they will use the Civil Service Commission as an excuse when they do not themselves wish to deal with any particular application. When asked to make an appointment or a promotion they will be able to say:	"We have nothing whatever to
do with this; the Civil Service Commission has charge of it." The hon. the Minister of Railway and Canals (Mr. J. D. Reid) says that in epite of the fact that Government railway employees are not to- be brought under the Civil Service Commission, he has given instructions to the general manager that patronage must be abolished and that no influence may be used by any candidates, friends of the Government or otherwise to impress upon the general manager the advantage of appointing this, that or the other man. The general manager is given authority to appoint men to positions without regard to political influence or to pressure from any person whatsoever. I naturally accept that

statement, of the Minister of Railways but it places the general manager of the Government railway system in a very peculiar position. Personally, I have not a great deal of acquaintance with him, but as far as I know 'he is a man of splendid ability and I believe he is very anxious to make a success of the railway system. It is hard for one to believe that a iman occupying that position would stoop to petty political partisanship and patronage in connection with the operation of the road. Yet, during the past two years, men in the employ of the Intercolonial, who would naturally be entitled to promotion, have been kept in their same positions while men new in the service have been put over their heads. That is not only true in regard to more important positions, but also in regard to the very lowest employees. Even in regard to temporary employees, the patronage curse is being forced upon the people in that portion of Canada. A man who comes with his saw and hammer, and who wants a job to help to erect or repair a small building, is not recognized by the man who has charge of the work unless he is armed with a certificate from the man who has the patronage. As evidence in support of that statement, I want to draw the .attention of the Government to a case that happened during the past winter in my own town. The Intercolonial required to erect a small roundhouse, or engine house, and the foreman was particularly anxious to get the work in progress as rapidly as possible. If the work were not proceeded with the engines would be left out in the cold and would suffer damage. The foreman tried to get men to go to work on that building. Finally he got a few men, and amongst them one man in particular who worked for four or five days. Then the foreman told him that unless he got a letter from the chairman of the patronage committee in the town of Sackville he could not continue on that work. How can the Government or the Minister of Railways and Canals expect us to accept the statement as to what they are going to do when we have such facts before us showing that instead of abolishing patronage, or making any attempt to abolish it, patronage is more rampant than ever and it is getting worse every day. In order to prove to this House the extent of the patronage evil in connection with the Intercolonial railway, and as an evidence why the Government railway system should be placed under the operation of this Bill, I will read the following affidavit:

Province of New Brunswick,
County of Westmoreland,	N.S.
I, Bernard Bowser, Builder and Contractor of the town of Sackville in the aforesaid county of Westmoreland, province of New Brunswick, being duly sworn make Oath and Say:-
That having been advised that skilled carpenters were required by the Canadian Government railway in the erection of a Roundhouse building at the railway yards in the town of Sackville aforesaid, I personally applied at the aforesaid premises of the railway for employment on or about the Thirtieth day of January A.D. 1918 and was employed and set to work by D. A. Seaman, foreman in charge of the said work, and continued at the said work for some five days.
That on the fifth day of my employment as aforesaid I was visited by the said Seaman, the foreman of the said work, and the following conversation took place between him and me:-
Seaman (foreman) "Can you get a recommendation?"
Bowser (employee) "It might be according to whom I got."
Seaman (foreman) "It is all right if it passes. Who are you going to get"?
Bowser (employee) "I might get Mr. Copp or Mr. McCord."
Seaman (foreman) "That won't do at all you will have to get some one from the Conservative Committee. Get Mr. Trites, some one that will pass it. It looks as if some of the party have written to Moncton saying you can not work without a recommendation. Can't you get Mr. Trites to give you a recommendation"?
Bowser (employee) "No, I wont ask Trites for any recommendation, the job is not worth more than a day's pay."
Seaman (foreman) "You had better leave your tools and see Mr. Trites, I do not want you to quit."
Bowser (employee) "No, I am not going to see Trites for any job."
Nothing further was said between Mr. Seaman and me on the occasion and I picked up my tools and quit the job and premises.
I am a native of the Parish of Sackville and have been active in my trade as a joiner and housebuilder for many years.
Sworn to at the town of Sackville, in the county of Westmoreland, province of New Brunswick this first day of April, A.D. 1918. Before me,
(Signed) Bernard Brown.
(Signed) A. W. Bennett.
A Commissioner for taking affidavits to be read in the Supreme Court of New Brunswick.
My reason for reading the affidavit is to demonstrate to my hon. friends who, I believe, are in, earnest in their determination to abolish the patronage evil, what is taking place on the Government system of railways, notwithstanding the fact that we now have a Union Government, and that one of the arguments in favour of the election of such a Government was that through its agency the country would be enabled to put an end to this evil. In the fall of 1917, we had the announcement that patronage was to he done away with, and yet

we find that as late as January, 1918, the system was still flourishing on the Government railways, and more particularly on the Intercolonial. In view of these facts, and, in view of the realization on the part of hon. gentlemen, not only from the Maritime Provinces, but from the rest of Canada as well, of the extent of the patronage evil, in view of the announcement that we were going to have a thorough housecleaning with respect to patronage, the Acting Minister of Finance will not be doing justice to himself, to the employees of the Intercolonial, or to the members of this House, if he fails to make provision whereby the employees of the Government Railway system shall be placed with respect to this matter in exactly the same category as the *civil servants in other departments of the public service.

speechtext: I wish to direct the minister's attention to a method of payment which is under consideration in the United States. On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Finance), Bill No. 85, to amend the Income War Tax Act, 1917, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-definitions:

Subsection 1 says:
Paragraph (e) of section two of The Income War Tax Act, 1817, chapter twenty-eight of the statutes of 1917, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:-
(e) "supertax" means the taxes authorized by paragraphs (b) to (m), both inclusive, of section four of this Act
Will my hon. friend state whait that means so that the public may understand it? It is not clear in the Bill.

In section 4 of the Act as it now stands there are paragraphs from (a) to (g) setting forth the tax and the amounts of income. Foi instance, by paragraph (b) the tax is 2 per cent on incomes exceeding $6,000 and not exceeding $10,000; paragraph (c) has reference to incomes exceeding $10,000 and not exceeding $20,000, and so on. Paragraph (g), which is the last clause in the old Act, provides a tax on incomes exceeding $100,000. We have divided incomes in excess of $100,000 into several clauses. For instance, on incomes from $100,000 to $200,000 there is a separate tax, and on incomes from $200,000 to $400,000 there is separate tax. That necessitated amending the paragraph.
It would be better to explain in general terms what is the meaning of .the word " tax " and what is the meaning of the word " supertax."
The present Bill provides for a normal tax of 4 per cent, which runs right through the whole list of taxable incomes.

My hon. friend has reduced the amount which by the Act of last year was exempted from taxation.

That exemption was $3,000 in the case of married persons and $1,500 in the case of unmarried persons without dependents. Those amounts are now reduced from $3,000 to $2,000, and from $1,500 to $1,000 respectively. Does not my hon. friend think, if he requires additional revenue that the small incomes should) be left just as they are and the higher incomes should be more heavily taxed? My hon. friend is aware that the cost of living is every day becoming a more and more anxious problem for families with average incomes. I do not know that the policy is wise of reducing the amount of exemption on incomes.
Mr. A. K. MA-CILEAN: My right hon. friend will remember that the tax is only 2 per cent upon incomes between $2,000 and $3,000 in the case of married persons, and between $1,000 and $1,500 in the case of unmarried persons. If he were considering this matter from the standpoint of revenue, it is quite clear that on the -smaller revenues we would derive the greater revenue. That is true, I think, of all countries in the world. Our rates of taxation on -the smaller incomes are less than they are in most -countries except the United States.
Sir WI Ll'RI I) LAURIER: Last year we agreed that the -average family should have a certain portion of its income exempt from taxation, and we placed that exemption at $3,000 in the case of a married person and $1,500 in the case of a -single person without dependents. My hon. friend is reducing that exemption, and it seems to me that in these days when the -cost of living is becoming increasingly heavy, he is going to get this revenue at the- expense of a good deal of comfort on the part of families with average incomes.
It is absolutely necessary that we have a revenue, and the Government were of the opinion it was desirable to reduce the amounts of exemption.
Why not increase the tax on the larger incomes?

My right hon. friend must not forget that the rate of taxation on the smaller incomes is very light, and that there is also a provision for granting an exemption of $200 for each child under sixteen years of age.

If it is in order at this point, I -should like to have a statement from the minister regarding the organization which he is providing for the collection of this tax. The organization which

he has already provided in our section of the country is wholly inadequate, the result being that I am satisfied the Government is going to lose thousands upon thousands of dollars this year and is going to create against this tax a sentiment which does not at the present time exist. There should be created from the very beginning an organization which will bring the very best methods to bear on the collection of this tax, and that, I contend is not being done. The gentleman who has been appointed as our collector in my district is one of the most competent men one could get in Canada, and he is doing his best to see that this tax is collected properly. But what are the conditions? I find to-day in his office in Regina from twenty-five to thirty thousand letters remain unanswered, simply because the staff and equipment is not sufficient. I understand the inspector has not been authorized to increase his [DOT]staff, and his quarters are wholly inadequate for transacting the business that is to be done in that province. The result has [DOT]been- -that when the returns come in, a great number of them are incorrectly made out, and the officer of the department, not [DOT]having the necessary staff and equipment to reply fully, -simply -sends bac-k the return, *and the recipient very often becomes rebellious and says he will not pay the tax at [DOT]all. I am satisfied that the people of -Saskatchewan are quite willing to pay this tax; in fact, they w-ant to pay it, but at the present rate of progress I do not think this tax will be collected in Saskat-4 p.m. chewan until next year's tax be

becomes due. I do not know what conditions are in other provinces, but that is the state of affairs in Saskatchewan. We [DOT]have the very best man possible at the head of the organization and he will do everything he can, but, without assistance it [DOT]will be quite impossible for him to give the results we want. I should like to know whether it is correct that the department do no-t expect to get this system of taxation- into complete operation for four or five years. I see no reason- for such a long delay as that, although I admit the Act will be difficult to administer, especially [DOT]in our part- of the country where probably more than a third of our population are foreigners, many of whom are liable to this tax. They are farmers, however, and are not banking their money, and some very complete organization will have to be devised to reach them.

I aim instructed by the officers of the department that the

inspector for Saskatchewan has ibeen given all the assistance he has asked for. There has been some trouble in obtaining suitable premises, and I shall be very glad to take into consideration what my hon. friend has said, and ascertain whether additional help is required. The department, of course, proposes to enforce the Act at once. My honourable friend's suggestion that it is going to take four or [DOT]five years to put the Act into effect is not correct. Probably he has heard some one remark that it will take a long number of years to have the Act working properly, [DOT]but that has been the experience in all countries. It is stated that it took Great Britain twenty-five years to approximate efficiency in the administration of their Income Tax Act, and the same is said of the United States. Difficulties and confusion will doubtless arise m Canada for the first few years, but I hope that gradually we .shall be able to develop an efficient and capable organization for the administration of this Act.
(Mr. COWAN: I am not blaming the Finance Department altogether. I have seen the deputy minister several times about the conditions out there, and I wish to repeat that the quarters provided are not at all satisfactory. Last year the same quarters were hired by the Imperial Oil company, and they got out because they could not keep the place heated. They had seven coal oil stoves going all winter to keep the place warm, and the staff naturally fell sick. Now we do not want anything like that.
Why is the unmarried woman on a different footing from the married woman?

There is no inequality. The unmarried and the married woman have the same exemption. " Married " includes both male and female. The married woman is exempt up to $2,000 and the unmarried up to $1,000.
iMr. J. H. 'SINCLAIRs I understand that, but I want to know why an unmarried woman should have to pay a larger tax than a married woman. A married woman has a husband to take care of her, and is in a much better position to pay than the unmarried woman.
Mr. DuTREMRLAY:	Paragraph (i) of
section 1 says:
"Dependent child" means a child under twenty-one years of age dependent on his parent for support. *
In some provinces, in Quebec, for instance, there is a law compelling children to provide for the support of their father or mother or grandfather or grandmother. Would it not therefore be wise to add a definition of the word " dependent " somewhat to this effect:	"relatives who are
dependent upon the taxpayers for support according to the law of each province."

That matter was considered very thoroughly at the last session of Parliament when the income tax was introduced. It may be possible that the tax may be onerous on unmarried persons who may have to support relatives or other persons, but it is- impossible to draft a provision providing for these exceptional cases.
Is the income of a man and his- wife regarded as one income or as two separate incomes?
As two incomes.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-par, relating to- payments at source:

How are you going to determine whether the child undeT sixteen years of age is dependent upon the taxpayer for support? Would it not toe toetter to take for granted that every child under sixteen is dependent on his parents for support? Otherwise the onus is thrown on the parent or on some one else to prove that the child is dependent.
There might toe oases where children, were in receipt of a large income from a trustee or something of that kind.

That is one of the difficult cases which the minister says cannot be provided for. If we are going to exempt the taxpayer $200 foT each child under sixteen, why not come out and say so flat-footedly? As the Act now stands, the department must obtain proof that the child is dependent on its parents- for support.
Mr. A. K. -MACLEAN: I think it is clear enough. I do not think it would be wise to- amend the section along the lines suggested toy my toon, friend. There may be other cases than the one I cited a moment ago, tout I really do not think there will be any difficulty in administering the Act in that respect.

Will the minister tell me why, under section 27, judges' incomes are not taxable?

Mr. A. K. MAC'LEAN: Would my hon. friend renew his question when we come to that section?
Mr. McMAiSTER: )I notice that by section 2 there is an exemption of $200 for every child under 16. Might I ask the minister whether he has considered the advisability of raising that age to, say, 18? There are a great number of people of moderate means who are doing their best to have their children finish their high school courses and it is rarely that children of 16 have finished with the high school. I would suggest that it would be advisable to Taise the age to 18. The minister would still be protected to the extent that the child must be dependent on the parent. The loss of revenue would not be considerable and it would be a great help tr people of moderate means who are endeavouring to give the best possible education to their children.

That matter was considered by the Government. A great deal could be said in favour of the suggestion but all exemptions and rates of taxation are arbitrary as a rule and suggestions are easily made in regard to them. The Government were of the opinion that 16 was the proper age to which to apply the exemption.
On section 3-income tax:
Mr. NIiCKLE: Will the minister be good enough to give me an explanation, because I have not been able to think of one, why it is that the incomes of husband and wife are treated as one. I think that in the working out of this Act, the country is losing considerable money owing to a married couple being entitled to double exemption. If there is any reason for the law being drafted as it is now, I would like to know what it is, and if the reason does not seem to be one that the House should approve, I would like to know if the minister would consider an amendment to the provision so that the exemption given to married people is only applicable to the income of one and not to the income of both.	,

That is a matter that had the consideration of the Government in the preparation of this Bill and they concluded that it was not advisable to amend the Bill in the direction suggested a;, tnis present session of Parliament. The chief reason is that a woman is a separate individual, as is a man, and in a country where we propose giving woman the franchise, just as we do a male person, I think

the argument is very strongly in favour of treating their incomes as separate. That is the general principle upon which the Government decided not to treat the incomes as one.
I do not think the philosophy of the minister's statement will stand criticism. He says the reason the exemption is given is because a woman is a separate entity before the law, as is also a man.
Might I ask the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) to speak a little slower and) a little louder because we want to hear what he is saying on this side of the House?

I say that I do not think the philosophy of the minister's statement will stand criticism. If I understood him correctly, he said that the reason that a separate exemption was given to a married man, and also to a married woman, was that the married woman was an entity before the law as was also the man. I cannot dispute that because to dispute it would lead one into a ridiculous position. We all accept that, but if a married woman is an entity before the law, and also a married man, why should the married woman get a married woman's exemption and the married man also get a married1 man's exemption when the responsibility for the maintenance of the family is on the married man and is not on the married woman? As the law stands at the present time, if a woman is unmarried, and has therefore no family responsibility, she is entitled to an exemption of $1,000, but if she marries and has an income, I think under the present Act, of $1,450, or of less than $1,500, she is entitled to exemption up to $1,500 and her husband is similarly entitled to exemption. I opposed this principle of the Act when it was introduced last session, emphasizing, as best I could, that I thought in exemption given to married people the exemption should only apply up to .the aggregate of the two incomes. In other words, if the combined income amounted to $1,500, exemption would 'be given under the present Act up to that amount. But if the combined income reached $2,000 then an income tax should be paid on the difference between $1,500 and $2,000. My experience during the past summer has convinced me that the contention I raised in the House last year is sound if the object of the Government is to get money.
Suppose there should be a couple, a man who had an income of say $3,500, and whose

wife had an income of something over $2,500. The combined income, we will say, was $6,000, and under the law as it stood last year each was entitled to an exemption of $3,000. That is .the woman paid no income tax, and the man only paid income tax on $500. Let us suppose the particular family I mention had no children, the result would be that a married man and woman without children get an exemption of $5,500, whereas these same people if unmarried would only get a small exemption granted to them, under the Act as d^awn last year, $1,500 each, and this year, of $1,000 each. I eay it is not sound finance and it is bad in principle, if the object is to get money, and I say it for the reason that I believe this income tax has come to stay, and in my judgment if the practice continues of treating ae separate the incomes of married men and women, there are going to be a good many incomes in this country divided into two parts to the extent at least of the exemption granted the woman, for the purpose of saving the income tax which she otherwise would have to pay. For instance, let me give an example: Suppose for the sake of my argument, a married man's income was just over $10,000 and suppose that the husband wants to get rid of the surtax, he transfers securities of such a value that it will bring an income to his wife of $1,450, and in that way she is entitled to exemption because being a married woman her income is less than $1,500, and he gets rid of the extra tax because he has $1,500 of the income applied to the wife, and leaves himself under the $10,000.
Mr. A. K. (MACLEAN. There is a provision in the Act against that.
Mr. N1CKLE:	There is a provision in
the Act against it, a provision in the Act does not amount to very much, because you cannot draw any Act to-day by which a husband cannot give to his wife a certain number of securities as a gift. I admit the principle of the Act says you must not do it, but there is no principle you can put in any Act which is going to prevent a married man, if he wants to do so, transferring certain securities over to his wife. The hon. gentleman says there is a provision in the Act against it. The forms that we had to sign last year certainly had nothing in them requiring one to declare that there had not been a transfer of property for the purpose of escaping the tax. As the practice, and as the law is at present, I submit the whole tendency is to deprive the State of some money that it legitimately should have, and to raise in
the minds of the people who have a taxable income, that they should look about in the hope that they may see a way of relieving themselves of some of the taxation. If the minister tells me he will not consider an amendment, nothing would be gained at this late hour of the session, by my moving an amendment, but I would like to urge upon him, as I did unsuccessfully urge upon his predecessor, that he give this matter consideration and impress upon him that I am looking at it from the point of view' in a part of the country where incomes are not large, and where people feel that all should bear equitably, the burden that is cast upon them, by this war.

It would be very difficult now to amend the Bill so as to cover the points raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Nickle). But I assure him that during the recess the matter shall have consideration by the 'Government. Personally, I am disposed to agree with the remarks of my hon. friend, and I think that probably at the next session of Parliament an amendment will be proposed to carry that idea into effect.

I am satisfied to have
bent the line, even if I have not broken it, but I hope that next session I shall succeed in breaking through.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):
speechtext: The tax on corporations is embraced within this clause. Suppose the tax is paid by the corporation, does that give an exemption to the man who holds the stock? To make myself clear I will give an example: Suppose John Smith has $5,000 of capital invested in Canadian Pacific stock, and the Canadian Pacific in the first place pays a tax of six per cent. Now, is any allowance made to Smith by reason of the fact that the corporation owning the stock has already paid that tax?
The income in that case is exempt from the normal tax only, which is four per cent.

Is not the tax six
per cent?

Four per cent is the normal tax upon incomes, as will be found in subsection a of section 4 of the Bill. The income tax upon corporations is six per cent, and when the corporation pays an income tax, the individual is exempt from the normal tax.

Before this clause carries I think we should pro-

test against the method prescribed of increasing the tax upon a corporation and not giving credit to the stockholder, which means ithe imposition of an extra tax on the latter. There can he really no question on that point. A corporation, under this clause, is called upon to pay six per cent upon its total net income. It distributes part, perhaps the larger part, of that income among its stockholders, some of whom are not liable to income tax. The Government gets six per cent from the corporation, and to that no objection can he raised. But is the stockholder, who is liable for income tax, prepared to have a two per cent tax imposed upon his income in addition to whatever tax he may be subject? The man who holds bonds, mortgages, or other securities, is not subject to this disability; it is one peculiar to the holder of stock, and I cannot see the logical justification for such a measure.

Has the Acting Minister of Finance taken any measures so as to protect Americans residing in this country from paying a double tax? I understand that at the present time there are a good many American citizens living temporarily in Canada who are earning wages and paying taxes in this country, and at the same time paying taxes in the United States; so that they are paying a double income tax. Has the Acting Minister of Finance had any communication with the United States Government so as to prevent the imposition of double taxes upon such persons?

That matter was a subject of negotiation between the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) and the officers of the Treasury Board at Washington a few days ago. The Minister of Finance advises me that he anticipates reaching some arrangement with the United States whereby persons might be relieved of the double income tax. And he also had a conference with the same officials in respect of the business profits tax, as there are instances where companies pay the business profits tax in Canada and in the United States as well. There is no provision in the Bill in respect of the matter, and it can only be overcome by arrangements reached by negotiations between the two countries. The matter of the double income tax received consideration at the last Imperial conference, and I understand it was decided to let the matter stand in abeyance until after the conclusion of the war. There is no doubt in the world that it is a great hardship, and should be eliminated in some way or other.

If I remember aright, the Acting Finance Minister in his Budget told us that the Government received practically ?385,000 from the insurance companies. I received the insurance blue book the other day, and looking over the statements of the insurance companies, I figured out that they were doing business to the extent of 8110,000,000 annually in Canada, and paid out in losses $43,000,000, leaving about $67,000,000 for expenses of operation. Of this the Government received only $385,000. It seems to me that is a very small amount.

The insurance
companies pay one per cent upon their net premiums.
The net premiums for fire, life and other insurance amount, I figure, to $110,000,000.
Life insurance is not included.
Why should it not be included as well as fire and other insurance?
I imagine it was deemed to be an unjust and unnecessary tax, and perhaps would do an injustice to people who were insured. The amount of the tax would probably have been added to the premium.

On the point raised by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn), the minister has not yet given a satisfactory explanation. In the income tax of last yeaT, where corporations were taxed at the rate of 4 per cent on all their profits and the balance distributed to shareholders, this 4 per cent was carried forward to the credit of the individual shareholder upon the dividend he had received. The present Bill raises the rate from four to six per cent. But on the two per cent additional the principle introduced into the Bill last year for some unexplained reason is now dropped. If it was good business and fair, even-handed justice to carry forward to the credit of the shareholder of the corporation or company the 4 per cent the argument is absolutely unanswerable, in my judgment, that now that 6 per cent is levied that 6 per cent should be carried forward to the credit of the shareholder, and he should not be subject to this extra 2 peT cent, which does not fall on any other class of the community only on corporations and joint stock companies. As the member for London said, if a man's income is invested in bonds, mortgages, or real estate, ot anything of that kind, it escapes. But, undeT this provision, as I understand

it-I may be wrong, but I have not heard anything to the contrary-while the tax is raised from 4 to 6 per cent, the shareholder in these corporations is only credited with 4 per cent instead of 6 per cent, which his stock has already paid before the dividends were distributed. I should like to ask the minister to justify that position if he can, so that I may be clear why the principle involved in the taxation of last year is being deviated frotm.

The point made by the hon. member for London is very substantial, indeed, and I am much impressed with it. I think probably at some future session of this Parliament some consideration will have to be given to that point. The necessities for revenue will justify the difference between the income tax-
It does not justify the inequality.
All taxation measures contain inequalities.

I would like the acting
minister to consider the phraseology of section 3, subsection (1), which reads:
There shall be assessed, levied and paid, upon the income during the preceding year of every person residing or ordinarily resident in Canada or carrying on any business in Canada, and upon the income received by any person from any source within Canada, the following taxes:
I put to the minister the case of a gentleman having an income of $10,000 arising in [Scotland and who is living in Canada. I would assume that that income is not taxed a second time. It is taxed 25 per cent, I think, in England. I notice that the minister said a moment ago

but do not know that I clearly grasped his meaning-that at the Imperial Conference it was. decided to prevent double taxation.

Efforts are 'being made to evolve some scheme to avoid double income tax, but no scheme or plan has yet been worked out. The purpose of the words "from any source" in the Bill is to make it possible for us to tax persons who earn an income within Canada, Ibut who live outside of Canada. We want to put ourselves in the same position as the United States in this respect.

If that is the intention, the Bill seems to Ibe unfortunately worded. The section as it Teads provides that the income must be obtained from any source within Canada. If it is obtained from a source in Scotland, it is not taxable?
No.
I was going to ask also if that is the intention of the Act. "From any source within Canada" would mean derived from a source within Canada, or as long as he received it while he is in Canada.
That was intended to impose taxation, upon incomes earned in Canada (by persons who do not live in Canada.

Since the hon. member for Kingston made his point in regard to the working out of this Bill, I have been doing some figuring, and would like to know whether the results, are correct or not. Take for instance the income of $10,000 in the ease of a married man. There would be an exemption, deducted from that of $1,500, leaving $8,500 subject to a 2 peT cent assessment, which would be $170. Then the income would Ibe subject to a .further tax after another exemption of $3,000 of 4 per cent on $5,500, which would be $220. In addition to that there would be a supertax of 2 per cent on $2,500, the balance of income over $6,000, .amounting to $50. Adding these three amounts, $170, $220 and $50, the tax on a married man with an income of $10,000 would :be $440.
Suppose a man's estate is in stocks and bonds., half of which he transfers to his wife. Each has then an income of $5,000, and would pay 2 .per cent on $3,500 and 4 *per cent on $500, or $90 each, a total of $180 *as against $440 if the estate had not been divided. The member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), who is a good lawyer, says that it [DOT]is possible to drive a wedge into the Act in [DOT]this respect. Is the argument of the member for Kingston sound, and are my figures correct?

The member for *Kingston properly stated the facts, but I [DOT]was unable to follow the figures given by [DOT]my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow); I did not [DOT]hear them. Section 4 of the Income War [DOT]Tax Act provides that any person who after *the 1st day of August, 1917, reduced his [DOT]income by transfer or assignment of any property, real or personal, to Ms wife or [DOT]to any members of his family shall nevertheless .be as liable to the tax as if such [DOT]transfer or .assignment had not been made. [DOT]The income from any property so transferred is treated as the income of the husband, notwithstanding the transfer.
Mr. MeMASTER:	In view of the fact
that we have to get money, the larger incomes should be more heavily taxed than

they are -by this proposed measure. The reply made by the Acting Minister of Firn-ance the other evening when I brought this [DOT]matter up was that although the British taxes are a great deal heavier than ours- $3,000 on an income of $10,000 in Great [DOT]Britain as against $400 or $500 on the same income here-we must not forget that the customs tariff imposes a very substantial indirect burden upon the people. In that I agree, but that is not the question. Money has to be found, and after we tax certain yearly incomes more or less lightly, we are in respect of taxation on the higher incomes, really taxing the luxuries and superfluities of life which a few people have but which the great masses of the people have not. To tax more heavily these higher incomes is the proper system of direct taxation to be followed at this time. I urge the Acting Minister of Finance to amend the Act so that the larger incomes will he taxed, perhaps not as heavily as they are in Great Britain,but at least more heavily than they will he taxed if this Act is passed in its present form. The minister will probably say that there is a great deal in my argument and that next year he may have to adopt my suggestion. He is running the risk of becoming known as the minister of good intentions rather than the Acting Minister of Finance. The poor people of this country, who are paying taxes on tobacco and tea, expect the Government to carry out the promise they made at the last election to stand for the conscription of wealth as well as for the conscription of men, and to carry it out as fearlessly with regard to wealth as they seem inclined to carry it out with regard to men. I believe that in this respect I voice, however feebly, the views of the people at large.

Being one of those who may be classed among the poor men who will help to pay these taxes-, in any arguments that I make I shall not be accused of defending the rich man. The Acting Minister of Finance read a statement the other evening showing the amounts paid here by way of income tax compared with those paid in the United States. We must not forget our geographical relation to the United States. England's large incomes have been worked up during a long period of years, while large incomes in this country are of very recent date. If you make the income tax in Canada lafger than it is in the United States, those who receive the larger incomes here may go to the United (States-it is just as warm there as

it is here; it is quite as comfortable a place to live in, and we are accustomed to the habits of their people. ' Most of the large incomes earned in this country are *derived from industrial pursuits. If a man whose income is very large is taxed too heavily, he is induced to put his money into Government bonds, which are not taxed, and to let the wheels of industry stand still. No greater calamity could overtake this country than that these large incomes should he put into Government bonds and the wheels of industry not kept moving after the war is over. Heavy taxes are now imposed under the Business Profits War Tax Act. If we continue to increase that tax we hamper a great many industries which have not yet been able to build up sufficient reserve to carry them through the hard times which will prevail after the war. So with income tax; there is a limit to the tax that we should impose on the income of the so-called rich man.
From the table which the acting minister put on Hansard the other evening, I noticed that the taxation on income up to $1,000,000 is higher in Canada than in the United States. Practically no one in this country is receiving an income of $1,000,000; indeed, there are in this country very few people receiving an income of more than $100,000, and yet our taxation on incomes up to $100,000 is considerably above the tax in the United- States. Nearly all the men in Canada who are deriving large incomes are deriving them from the risks they have run and the strenuous exertions they have made to establish industries in this country. The man who is prepared to take chances in investing his money to build up industries in this country deserves what he gets. I would ask any of my hon. friends who are anxious to see how much money they can make in industries, just to invest money in them, and see what happiness they will have after they have been in the business for a while. I give credit to men who have put their money together and started an organization. I do not understand the feeling that exists in this country against corporations. Corporations are only unions of individuals who have had faith enough to put money into one man's hands for investment in an industry which he manages. If he makes a success of it and they begin to make money they deserve it, 'because they have taken a risk. For one corporation that succeeds in this country three fail to accomplish their purposes, so that there is a big risk in putting your money into industries. It is unwise for us to keep harping against the so-called

large incomes and to keep taxing them out of this country, because it will be a great detriment to Canada to drive men into investing their money in Government bonds or out of the country altogether.
(Mr. McMA-STER: I have mo desire to tax capital out of this country, but I have a desire to see some basis of equality of sacrifice between the people of smaller incomes, whose sons have gone to the front and who remain and are taxed on their simple luxuries at home, and those .people of large incomes, whose sons have also gone gallantly forward,	but who remain
with as many luxuries, as great incomes from a	material standpoint
as they had before the war, and many of whom find that their fortunes have been enormously increased on account of the war. We ought, as far as possible, to have an equality of sacrifice between the different classes of this country. Suppose I said to you, Mr. Chairman, that we should judge of the sacrifice of men between ourselves and the United States. We would point out that they should send overseas an army of 5,000,000 men to be on an equality with the man-sacrifice demanded in this war. The argument is, therefore, not altogether sound that we should look merely to the United States to see whether our taxes are on an equality with theirs. I think better of the wealthy men of this country than to imagine that they will object to heavy taxation so long as that heavy taxation is distributed justly and evenly, and I do not think, if they are heavily taxed, they will skedaddle to the United States.
My hon. friend has much greater faith in humanity than 'I have.
Perhaps I have.

So- far as the sacrifice
of the rich man since this war started is concerned, II venture to s-ay that if my hon. friend picks out man for man in this country, he will find that the so-called rich man has sacrificed just -as much, both physically through his family and so far as his means are concerned, as any other class of people. Not only is that the case, but the rich men have been the great subscribers to all the benevolent funds that have been started in this country. Otherwise, those funds could not succeed. Let my hon. friend pick out, if he will, the so-called rich men in this country, and he will see how many of them have sent their sons and brothers to the front just as freely as the poorest man in Canada.

I said that they had
gallantly sent their sons to the front.

The question raised by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and -the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is a most interesting one, and I am much surprised that no hon. member from the Western Provinces has so far taken, part in the debate. Before the last elections were held, there was a convention, which was forgotten by most people, but which I remember. I refe-r to the convention held in the city of Winnipeg. I understand that certain members of this Government and certain other hon. members sitting in this House were present at that convention, at which one of the main planks of the platform of the so-called western party was conscription of wealth. Where is conscription of wealth? How has that promise been fulfilled? The Acting Minister of Finance makes the proposition of taxing incomes up to 50 per cent and not above. That is not sufficient. Conditions throughout the world are to-day most extraordinary and exceptional, and a Government that wants the actual condition of things and order to be maintained in this country must see that the burden of taxation is evenly and fairly distributed amongst the different classes of our people. Is that the case to-day? I claim it is not. After this Bill is passed, whenever a poor man who earns a few dollars a day goes to the grocery store at the corner, he will have to pay taxes for -al'1 kinds of commodities of which he is in absolute need. He will have to pay taxes on tea, matches, tobacco, playing-cards. This poor man who, by working probably . ten or twelve hours a day, is able to earn $2.50 or $3, will be spending practically one-half of his salary in paying taxes. In comparison with that man, let us take a man like Sir Joseph Flavelle. How is he taxed by this Government? How are Mackenzie and Mann taxed by this Government? How are those millionaires who bought and bribed the press of this country during the last election taxed? How is the wealth of our country taxed? How are those people who claim to own this country taxed by the present Government? They are not taxed at all-and why? Because this Government does not dare to do its duty.
The Acting Minister of Finance, whose Liberal principles are well known, who used in this House to profess real Liberalism, who last year got up in this House and said in reply to the Minister of Finance in the then Tory Government, "Taxation is not

t
equal in this country"-what changes has he brought about? I have listened to all his speeches this year, and from a Liberal speaker he is changing into a speaker more Tory than his predecessor ever was. We do not want any more Tory theories in this country. 'The Canadian people stand for Liberalism and democracy. The only Tory country left in the universe to-day is the one against which we are directing all our efforts-Germany-and the only Tories left in the world to-day are the Germans. I do not wish to join them. I wish to remain with the real Liberals, the Liberals who say that when people are to be taxed, they shall be taxed according to their means and not according to their power or influence.
When it comes to the poor man 5 p.m. in this country, with little money and1 no influence, the Minister of Finance .goes into his pockets and takes a few pennies he has, taxes his tobacco, his matches, his tea and his other necessities.
