speechtext: Is that satisfactory to the hon. gentleman?

Yes.
On section 4-Judges' salaries, retiring allowances or annuities exempted-:
The language in paragraph (k) is rather complicated-, does it mean that the salaries of judges are not taxable?

Under the Judges' Act the incomes of judges are exempt from taxation, and it was desired to state that exemption in the present Bill for the guidance of the officers of the department who will be charged with administering the Act when it goes into force throughout Canada. This provision does not change the law in any respect.

The provision has been framed in a rather roundabout and complicated way. All I want is to make it perfectly clear what is regarded as income and what is not regarded as such. In this connection I do not think any definite judicial opinion has been expressed as to whether the indemnity of members of Parliament is regarded as income for the purposes of taxation. It would be well perhaps for members to know whether it is or not.

The indemnity of members is subject to the income tax. Section 3 of the Judges' Act, which grants exemption from taxation, is as follows:
The salaries and retiring allowances, or annuities, shall he payable by monthly instalments, and shall be free and clear of all taxes and deductions whatsoever imposed; under any Act of the Parliament of Canada.

Under that I would apprehend the allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick of $5,000 a year for acting as deputy

of the Governor General-that is, he comes down, I believe, once a year and nods his head to a few Bills, for which he gets $5,000-will escape taxation although it is income.
No, I hardly think that.

Yes, it is not salary in the real sense of the term. And his allowance of $2,500 will escape taxation also. Why should judges' salaries be exempted from taxation? I am opposed to the whole thing. I do not believe it is democracy at all. Why should a judge's salary escape taxation? Can he not stand on the same plane as anybody else, and pay his share of the burdens imposed by the war. It seems ridiculous to me; I am opposed to it, and will test the sense of the Committee by a vote if I can get the necessary support.

As every member of this House has to pay income tax, there is no reason why the judges should be exempt. The ordinary man has to go out and earn money to help to pay the salaries of judges, and it seems to me they should be made subject to the tax just the same as anybody else. I intend to move that paragraph (k) in clause 4 be struck out.
It would not help the situation any to strike this paragraph out.

It would show that we are opposed to this exemption.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN; Under a separate Act of Parliament the salaries and retiring allowances or annuities of judges are not subject to any taxation by this Parliament. Paragraph (k) was inserted in the Bill to make all the officers who will be engaged in the administration of the Act cognizant of the fact, and if the paragraph is struck out it does not change the situation at all.

It was not the
purpose or intention of this section to remit taxation. Under the Judges' Act their
salary is exempt from taxation under thie or any other Act. At any rate I propose asking the committee to permit me to withdraw this paragraph (k) altogether. I propose. submitting the matter on an amendments of the Judges' Act to my colleagues.
Hear. hear.

I have often wished that I had studied law. If I ever get time I intend to study it just as a pastime. The Judges' Act has been quoted as a reason why salaries of judges cannot be touched.
I do not suppose that the Judges Act, providing that their salaries should be exempt from taxation, while it had reference to Acts already passed, was intended to apply to Acts that might be passed in all futurity. Surely it never meant that.
If you can provide in any Act that a certain thing can be done notwithstanding anything in any other statute, surely you can put the same proviso in this Bill in regard to the salaries of judges, and say that they shall be taxed notwithstanding anything in any other statute. Apart altogether from that, under the War Measures Act, by which it seems we can move the Atlantic to the Pacific, and the Pacific to the Atlantic, the Rocky mountains to the sea, and the plains down to the ocean, there is power enough to put. a tax on judges salaries. Why should not a tax be placed on their salaries? That is a question which every person will ask.
Even on the salary of a Chief Justice.

Even a Chief Justice- if I might even mention that title-should be taxed, and a certain five thousand dollars should have a supertax on it. However, I won't talk about that, I may be called to order. Allow me to point out what sacrifices men are making in this country. Take', for instance, a farmer who, with the help of his only son, and of his whole family as well, by working from daylight until dark, is making possibly $1,500 or $1,600 a year. That son has to go to the war as .provided by the recent order. That is all right. But that will mean for that farmer and his family a lessened revenue by five or six hundred dollars a year. He is not only sacrificing his flesh and blood, or at least offering it for sacrifice overseas if that may be necessary; but his revenue is being depleted by the absence of his son by five or six hundred dollars, and he is a poor man, W^hile he is making that sacrifice not only on the battlefield hut in a monetary way as well, we are told that we must

not touch the salaries of these gentlemen who remain and sit on the Bench. I, for one, .say it is not democratic, fair, or reasonable in any sense that if those gentlemen do not voluntarily contribute as other men contribute, then I say by an Act of this House they should be forced to contribute as other men drawing like salaries are forced to do. Their future has Been well 'looked after by Parliament. A certain number of lawyers in the House of Commons are always anxious to look after any .of the fraternity. They have provided fair-sized' salaries for the judges, and they have made provision for the time when those judges reach old age or think that they should retire-and some of them have retired on good, fat allowances and have taken, up much more strenuous work than that which they performed on the bench, and at larger salaries than they formerly received. It is said that men who occupy judicial positions should not pay anything by way of taxation towards the expenses of this war. That view is absolutely indefensible, and, if put to a vote of the people, would not get the support of a corporal's guard outside of those members of the legal fraternity who look forward to the day when they shall occupy a position on the bench.

This question, is not at all one-sided. For a time I was a judge in a small way, but I am a judge no longer, so I cannot be accused of partiality. It is m the interests of this great, democratic country that judges should be absolutely independent. Judges are paid high salaries so that, as far as money is concerned, they shall be absolutely beyond temptation. That is a good thing for the country. Our judges are splendid men; they give fair decisions and administer the law as they understand it. T know of no case in which money con- . siderations has influenced any of ' our judges. They get good, fat salaries, and they are absolutely independent. Another thing that is in the interest of democracy is that the judges should not be dragged into political controversies. We have stripped them of the franchise; they may not express their opinion at the polls. It is highly desirable that they should' be absolutely independent. Considering them as a class, there are but a few judges in this country, and the few dollars that we would get by imposing a tax on their incomes would not amount to very much. I do not express these views because I believe that the judges should, be allowed to keep the few dollars which the imposition of the tax 
would involve. There is therefore another side to the matter which is of more importance to the country than the small amount of money we would get by assessing their incomes for this tax.

It is not a question of the few dollars that we would get; it is a question of the principle that'is involved. Why should the man earning a small salary be required to pay taxes while the judge, who is earning a large salary should be exempt? The unfairness of the suggestion will surely impress itself upon the people. The member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) believes that judges are given the large salaries so that they will not be subjected to temptation with regard to money. I recall a case where a judge was required to make restitution of $5,000 .that he had taken improperly. Moreover, we have the case referred to recently in this House- that of a gentleman, whose name I am not allowed to mention, who took at least $5,000 to which he had no claim. The payment of large .salaries to judges does not change their sense of humanity; so that the argument of the member for North Cape Breton does not hold. The man who draws a Government salary of $10,000 has just as much right to pay taxes as the man who draws $3,000 from an industrial organization. We want to be fair and just. The member for Kingston suggests that we should in a delicate way suggest to the judges that they pay these taxes, although they are not required to do so. I am afraid we would not increase the revenue very largely by that process. If the principle is right, then everybody should be taxed under the law. The amount of revenue we get in this case is not the point at issue, there is an important principle at stake.

I quite agree with the hon. member (Mr. Hocken) .that a principle is involved; if I did not feel that I should not be on my feet again. If I understand anything about the constitutional position of the judges under our British system, particularly in a democratic country, it is this: judges are supposed to be above and beyond governments and parliaments in so far as either governments or parliaments can in any way indirectly influence them by .passing legislation affecting their financial position in relation to their salaries. The very principle upon which the stability of our judicial system is based is this: when you appoint a judge you appoint him for life. You give him reasonable remuneration to prevent the possibility of his de-

siring to secure further financial assistance by improper methods, and you lay down in your statute that he shall not be taxable by the Government by virtue of any legislation passed subsequent to his being appointed to the bench.
When was that provision adopted-many years ago?
I am referring to the Revised Statutes of 'Canada, 1906.
That section is perhaps twenty-five or fifty years old.
If we should trace the section in all its history, I should not be surprised to find that it was taken from some British statute perhaps two hundred years ago.
We are at war now.

In the working out of our constitution to define the position of the judiciary, of the executive and of the legislature, an effort was made to put the judicial powers far beyond the interference either of the Government or of the legislature and the object sought was to give the judge sufficient remuneration to make him immune from temptation and to put him in such a position that no adverse Government, no body of legislators opposed to the man, could by duress-that is, by threatening to interfere with his salary by a tax-do something to impair his administration of justice. I argue that because by statute we said that the salary of a judge should be exempt* and because men were on that condition appointed to the bench, that that national obligation should be respected-because it is, in my judgment, a national obligation. The member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) says that it is not a contractual obligation. I meet my hon. friend by saying that it is a statutory contractual obligation, and that we should respect that obligation so far as the position of the judges now appointed goes. And the argument of the member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) falls to the ground when he says that members of the legal profession always rush to the defence of the judiciary because they hope sometime to reach the woolsack. My position is that I am willing that the Act be amended to provide that this income tax shall apply to the salary of any judge subsequently appointed. But I should be sorry to see this House or this Government lay down the principle that an obligation of the nation to the judges should be interfered
with, unless the judges were prepared to acquiesce. It is fundamental and a protection to democracy that judges should feel that their tenure of office is secure and that their promised emoluments are not subject to attack either by Government or by Parliament.

I want to refer to just one point in the argument of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). The hon. member put forward two grounds. One was a statutory ground, namely, that those salaries were granted to those men, and that there was a contractual or statutory obligation in connection therewith. I think that was the legal phraseology used to describe the operation. There was also a contractual or statutory obligation to pay certain members of the Civil Service who went oversea? their salaries in addition to their pay of rank as soldiers. Those civil salaries *were paid for a time when those men went overseas, but it has recently been, thought wise to break that contractual or statutory obligation to those men, who are overseas fighting and risking their lives for the judges who are here in safety and who, God grant, will all live to be one hundred or more years of age. The point was raised by the hon. member ifor North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) that the salaries of the judges were fixed at an amount which would place them above temptation. That point was also mentioned by the hon. member for Kingston. I am glad to hear that given as a reason. It throws a great deal of light on past history and past action in this House, because at various times, the salaries of judges have been increased.
I presume at the time the salaries were first fixed, the amount, for instance, $5,000, was considered sufficient to keep them honest; but when in the wisdom of Parliament, that was raised to $7,000, I presume it was thought absolutely necessary to give them another two thousand dollars if we wanted to keep them honest and to remove temptation from them. The simple explanation of any increase in the salaries of judges is: We must keep those judges above temptation; we must remove all temptations from them by raising their salaries so that they will not be tempted to go elsewhere for money. Has that been the result? Not that one would notice particularly. I have in mind a judge whose salary is fixed at a good figure-at least I would consider it a good figure if I was getting it. Of course,
I would not say that I was competent to earn any such salary. I do not object to judges getting generous salaries; I would like to see them all getting good salaries. But that was not considered, according to the argument of the hon. member for North Cape Breton, sufficient to keep this judge honest, and, therefore, he was given an additional sum for certain work which did not take him five minutes in the year, 
fcr signing his name once or twice for another party who might happen to be away fishing for the time being. Some four or five thousand dollars was given to him in that way to keep him above temptation. One wrould have thought a salary of $10,000, plus the additional amount to which I have referred, would have been sufficient to lift him clear above any possible temptation; but it did not, and another salary was created for certain duties which he had to perform in a far distant country. He was not to get this salary unless he performed those duties, it should not have been paid to him. There was only one reason why it should be paid to him. I am glad to note that it was not because he was justified in getting it or because he earned it, but it was granted and paid to him for two years in. succession in order to keep him above temptation. Read us not into temptation, but deliver us from judges.

I understood the hon.
member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) to say, in a very fervent manner, that taxes should, be imposed in accordance with the ability of a person to pay. That is a pretty sound Liberal principle; at least, it has been enunicated in that way here to-day, and it i-s one that I am entirely willing to accept. If we are going to proceed along that line, surely those men who are getting $10,000 :a year and who are relieved of many financial responsibilities which other citizens have to bear, should be willing to submit to this form of taxation. Am ordinary man, in business or in any profession, has sometimes to pay up to $1,000 or $1,500 a year for life insurance, if he wishes to take care of his family after his decease; but here we have a set of men who drew full salary as a pension, and who are not under the same financial obligation to take care of their families, because they may be expected to live at least until all their children are settled. There is another consideration. Most of the men who are appointed to the judiciary are men who .have been eminent in the legal profession. A man, who has had a good practice of the kind that most men have who get to be judges, should be able to put away a large sum of money. Such men are usually able to amass a considerable competence before they are appointed to the bench, so that on the_ grounds of relief from financial responsibilities that other men must carry, and on the salary they receive, and on the probability that they are fairly

well off to begin with, I do not see why we should exempt every one of them to the extent of $360 a year. My opinion is that any self-respecting man occupying the position of judge in this country would be not only willing but anxious that he and hie class should not be taken out of this Act' and exempted when all the other people of this country are being taxed in this time of national stress.

I brought up this matter at an earlier stage when the resolution was under diseueion, and I was met by the statement that there was a guarantee in the Judges' Act that the judges should be exempt from taxation. I have a profound respect for vested rights; I have a profound respect for a promise that has been made by a man, a Government or by anybody else, and since we have given the judges, foolishly I think, this exemption, I would not advocate the violation of our pledge.
I think the only reason why this exemption has been tolerated in the past is that we never understood it. There1 was no subh tax from which they could be exempt. They were not exempt from customs, they were not exempt from excise, but there was: a clause that they were exempt from taxes which had no existence whatever then. That being the case, there was nothing to draw public attention to it. I am content that we should keep faith with the judges. I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not in his seat, for I would have offered the suggestion that he should now at this session introduce a Bill to repeal that exemption clause in the Judges' Act, not as respects the judges of to-day

I would keep faith with them, because a bargain is a bargain, and even if it is a had bargain, or an imprudent bargain we must nevertheless stick to it-but to abolish that exemption as respects, any judge who may hereafter be appointed.

speechtext:
No, the freight rates were exactly the same. The order of the Board of Railway Commissioners, granting the railways an. increase of 15 per cent, became effective on the railways on a certain date, and on the same date a similar increase was made on the Government railway system. That was two months, ago. We got no benefit last year from that decision.
(Hon. gentlemen are aware that during the past year the several large railway corporations have been pressing the Railway Commission to allow them an increase of rates. From the statement I have presented in connection with the Government
railways, it must be apparent to every member of this House that they were justified in asking an increase. The Government railway system increased freight rates equally with other railways. Even though we have increased rates. I am not looking forward to any surplus; we expect to have a loss, and perhaps a very large one, during the coming year.
During the past year we have not undertaken any extensive new work, although we have been endeavouring to complete the works in process of construction. I am pleased to be able to say that we expect that the Halifax ocean terminals will be practically completed during the present fiscal year.' I am also glad to say that last year we used those portions of these new terminals which have been made available. Had those works not been undertaken, we would not have been able to handle the traffic that has developed at that port during the present war. I desire to emphasize that fact-it would have been impossible to have handled the freight and passenger traffic at Halifax if we had not had the new terminals now nearing completion. Then again, when the disastrous explosion occurred on December 6, last year, which destroyed the major portion of the other *docks, the fact that we had available a large portion of the new terminals saved the situation.

The deficit on this- railway during the last year amounts to $488,172, the largest in the history of the road. It has never been possible to make this railway pay, but at the time .of Confederation it was taken over and the Government has to operate it for the accommodation of the

I am pleased to say that this car ferry is in operation and is doing good work, it has been suggested that the railway on the island be changed from the present narrow gauge to the standard gauge, and I may say that it was the intention of the Government to consider this, in order that commodities shipped to and from the island could go through to their destination without transhipment. But owing to war conditions making the financial situation so, serious and so greatly enhancing the cost, it is impossible for the Government to go into the widening of the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway while the war continues. It is not merely a question of change of gauge; it practically means an entirely new railway, the complete replacement of all motive power and equipment, and the revision of curves and gradients so numerous on the island, and which, while suitable for the present light equipment, would never do for the heavier main-line motive power and rolling stock. It would mean an expenditure of at least $2,000,000, which cannot be entertained at this time.
Provident Fund.
The provident fund, which is an employees' pension department, to which the railway contributes $100,000 per year, had on its rolls 1,096 ex-employees, covering a period from 1907 to 28th February, 1918. Of this number 363 have died, and the remaining are receiving pensions which amount to $254,201.50.
Employers' Relief and Insurance Association.
This is a life and accident insurance organization supported by contributions from employees and $10,000 per annum contributed by the railway. During the past year 197 death claims and three total disability claims were paid, amounting to $76,000. Sick benefits to employees, medical and surgical attendance and other expenses in connection with the organization show a gross expenditure on this account of $30,783.51. These amounts are larger than previous years, owing principally to loss of life and injuries to employees in the Halifax disaster.
Canadian Railway Association for ' National Defence.
It might be well to mention at this point that, in my opinion, the operation of all the railway systems in the Dominion of Canada during the past year was the equal of, if not better than, that of any other railways on the continent; and I believe that the reason of this was the action of the ia,rge railway systems!-the Canadian Pacific railway, Grand Trunk railway, Grand Trunk Pacific railway, Canadian Northern railway and the Canadian Government railways-in joining together and forming an organization known as the Canadian Railway Association for National Defence. The association's executive committee on war and national defence is composed of the following persons: Lord Shaughnessy, Canadian Pacific railway; Howard G. Kelley, Grand Trunk railway; Sir William Mackenzie, Canadian Northern railway, and Alfred H. Smith, New York Central railway. In turn they organized an administrative committee to deal with the situation, composed of the following:	U. E.
Gillen, chairman; D. B. Hanna, A. E. Warren, C. A. Hayes, Sir George Bury, F. F. Backus, E. D. Bronner, J. H. Walsh and A. E. Warren, the -latter representing the Minister of Railways.
The Prime Minister explained this organization on Wednesday last, and I will not go into further details. We have reports from this organization day by day. During the past year the different railway companies have been working together practically as one organization, and the results have been as stated by the Prime Minister.

All orders have been given for cars and engines. Before ordering these cars, I conferred with the Canadian Northern railway, the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Government railway management, and they all agreed that this additional equipment should be ordered and secured at the earliest possible moment.
I shall now refer, very' briefly, to other phases of departmental activity.
Halifax Ocean Terminals.
The work on the Halifax ocean terminals has been continued, the present status being as follows. Grading is practically completed; overhead bridges carrying streets across the railway are all practically completed. Sufficient trackage has been installed to serve the two temporary sheds built last year, and two large temporary sheds on pier A, which were rushed to completion after the explosion of December 6 last, and which are now in use, together with a 100-car team track yard for serving the north end of the city. The placing of concrete blocks for quay walls is practically completed, and there remains only a small quantity of concrete work and granite facing in order to finish the quay walls. The filling has been proceeded with, but there still remains over 500,000 yards of filling to be placed behind the quay walls. Arrangements are being made for the erection of a temporary station and the construction of coach yard with coach-cleaning and repair facilities for the handling of the passenger traffic business of the city,

as North street station and facilities are not suitable since 'the explosion for the carrying on.of this work.
I may also state that the .station was very badly damaged, and that we must get away from it at the earliest possible moment. The contractor claims that the new station will be ready for ue about the month of September next, when iwe shall run all trains into the new terminals.
Halifax Disaster and Restoration.
In the disaster of 6th December, 1917, at Halifax 56 employees and 10 pensioners of the Canadian Government railways were killed, and 2 employees afterwards died from injuries received in the explosion. Thirty employees were killed while on duty. Of the 1,078 employees of the railway living in Halifax and Dartmouth at the time of the explosion, investigation showed that only-157 were comparatively unaffected by the disaster; 107 who owned their own homes, and 165 who were tenants had their property totally destroyed; 432 had properties more or less, damaged, requiring at least considerable repairs. Later on, the Rehabilitation Branch of the Relief Committee, in their housing programme, agreed to provide at least 84 temporary houses for employees of the railway. The following railway and 56 freight oars of other lines, valued at $50,000, were destroyed.
Removal of wreckage and clearing tracks and replacing various electrical lines throughout Richmond yard and North street

station "will have cost, .when complete, roughly, $100,000.
One hundred and three Government railway cars of passenger class, and 9 cars of other lines' of the same class were damaged to an estimated extent of $60,000.
Thirty-seven Canadian Government railway and 56 freight cars of other lines valued. at $50,000, were destroyed.
One hundred and twenty Canadian Government railway and 222 freight cars of other lines were damaged to approximately $54,000.
Four Canadian Government railway locomotives suffered, damages estimated to amount to $6,000.
Canadian Government railway steamer McKee was also damaged and is now under repair.
The Willow Patk shops, consisting of roundhouse, machine shop; power plant, planing mill, car repair shop, coaling plant and ash pit, and stores and office 'building suffered severely. These damages have been estimated at $130,000.
The shipping facilities at piers Nos. 2, 3 and 4 and the adjacent freight shed and other buildings, are all much damaged, but they have been nearly completely repaired. The elevator has been repaired.
The piers at Richmond are all wrecked and some are totally destroyed. Pier No. 9 has been repaired and is in use.
In order to obtain relief as quickly as possible from the effects of the damage to the various shipping facilities, the construction of two large sheds on pier A at the ocean terminals site was rushed to completion at the same time as repairs were being made to the previously used wharves, etc. These sheds are now in operation and the repair work is also practically complete. In addition to the work on the railway properties, the Restoration Organization have carried out the repairs to H.M.C. naval dockyard and to the naval hospital, under arrangement with the Department of the Naval Service. This work will co^t about $205,000. The estimated cost of reconstruction on Canadian Government railways' properties is estimated to be about $1,250,000. Of this amount $850,000 will have been spent by March 31. Or in other words, the loss to the country on account of the Halifax disaster, so far as the Canadian Government railway system is concerned, is $1,250,000.
Hudson Bay Railway.
We have expended upon this enterprise up to February 28 of this year, the sum of $20,161,000, of which $13,814,000 was on
account of the railway, and $6,347,000 was on account of the harbour and terminals at Port Nelson. The latter .sum includes expenditures incurred in the purchase of steamships which are now in general service throughout the year, as well as the valuable plant at Port Nelson. During the past year the construction of the bridge over the Nelson river at Kettle rapids has caused the suspension of tracklaying. The north and south arms of the bridge were connected up in December and tracklaying can be continued this season. The grading between Kettle rapids and Nelson was completed and train-filling and ballasting at various points along the line was continued. At Port Nelson a restricted programme was- followed, in which materials and supplies.on hand were utilized. Owing to the general shortage of ocean tonnage no further shipments were made to the Bay during the season. The island crib-work was extended and dredging continued.
Prince Edward Island Car Ferry.
The total amount expended upon this work has been about $2,875,000. We are asking for a further appropriation of $65,000 to cover certain minor additions which have been deferred until actual operating conditions could be observed. The main contracts for the construction of terminals were completed during the season of 1017 and the steamer " Prince Edward Island " was placed cn the route in the beginning of October. All freight offering has been satisfactorily handled since that time.
Canals, General.
But little new construction work was done on the canals during the past year, and even minor improvements and works of maintenance were restricted to essentials. Our only appropriations on capital account for the year just closed were for the Welland ship canal and the Trent canal. Upon the ship canal the work done during the year was of an emergency repair nature, being occasioned by clay slides, one of which destroyed the temporary crossing provided for the Queenston road, and the other, by its proximity to the existing canal, was considered so menacing as to require immediate attention. Construction work under the several contracts was suspended throughout the year. As there appears to be no possibility of resuming this work for some years, the several contractors have requested that they be relieved of further responsibility with respect thereto. Equitable arrangements have been concluded with several of them for the surrender of their contracts, and it is hoped

that mutually satisfactory arrangements will shortly be completed with the others.
On the Trent system we had a number of contracts nearing completion on the On-tario-Riee lake division, upon which work was continued with some hope of clearing them up during the year. Owing chiefly to labour conditions, slow progress was made, and although we shall be able to open this division for navigation this spring, each of the contractors has a few months' work to do. The Grand Trunk railway are proceeding with their high-level bridge at Gampbellford, and the barrier created by their present low-level structure will be removed during the early spring.
On the Severn division, two contracts were in force. As this division cannot be brought into service until another section, not yet under contract, has been completed it was deemed advisable to close down work upon section 3, which connects Lake Couchiching with the Severn river. On section 2, all efforts were concentrated upon the completion of the power house and dam at Swift rapids, with auxiliary works related thereto. This structure was completed with great benefit to the power situation in the surrounding neighbourhood.
I do not think I can add anything to what I have already said, hut I shall ba very glad, indeed, to give full information on any questions that are asked.
Was that large tract of land at Rideau junction included in the bargain with the Canadian Northern railway?
That land was purchased by the Canadian Northern Railway system; it was deeded to that railway, and is now owned by the Crown.

I am very glad to hear that, as it is one of the most valuable pieces of land in that section of the country. I trust the Government will not allow it to lie waste as it has done for the last five years. It has been nothing hut an eyesore in the past. The buildings that were on it were pulled down, and the land could not have looked worse if the Germans had passed over it. Part of the land has been cultivated this year, but very little, and I trust the Government will see to it that this valuable tract of land, comprising eight or nine hundred acres, will be used not only for railway purposes but cultivated to the very best advantage. I should also like to know whether any improvements will be made through that section.

Any improvements along the Canadian .Northern will be made

through the board of directors which is now operating the Canadian Northern Railway system, and not through the staff of the Railway Department at Ottawa.
The sooner the improvements are made the better, because that part of the road is in a very bad state.

At the present time the Government would have no say in such matters as the hon. member has mentioned. But I would suggest that from now on, as. this railway belongs to the people, any hon. member who thinks improvements should be made on the line in any part of his constituency should communicate with the head of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Later on, of course, he should communicate with the head of the reorganized board, which the Prime Minister said would be constituted at a date not far distant.
I can assure the minister I will cheerfully do anything I can for the benefit of the road.
What use is (being made of the land my hon. friend spoke of just now?

The Canadian Northern directors will use it as they think best, but I was suggesting that if any hon. member sees land going to waste belonging to the railway, or the necessity for 'mprovements on the line in his constituency, he should communicate with Mr. Hanna, the general manager of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Of course, if he .should write to me as Minister of Railways and Canals I shall be very glad, indeed, to forward the communication, but -I wish to emphasize that the management will be by the board, and not by the Department of Railways and Canals.
I think my hon. friend mentioned .something about buildings at Rideau Junction.
No, there are only ties there.

I think the statement that has been .made by the minister is .satisfactory. I should like to know whether the Government railways have charged the same rate for the conveyance of troops as the other roads. In other words, is the deficit on the Intercolonial and other Government roads partly attributable to the fact that Canadian troops have been carried at a lower rate than on the other roads in Canada?	-

I understand that the Government railway system charge.- the same rates as the other roads, with this exception, that ours is the longer haul, and consequently the proportion we get of the through rate is greater. The amount, we receive is in proportion to the haul.

Is the minister sure of that? The Government haul may or may not be the longer haul. Let us suppose the traffic originates in British Columbia, comes partly over the Government road, and then over the Grand Trunk to Montreal, and is there transferred to the Intercolonial. Will the minister say that that traffic is in the ordinary proportion as between two privately owned roads?
That is the information I have from my officials.

I have been informed that a number of cheques were issued by the Department of Railways and Canals during December last in settlement of claims for right of way through Carleton county. Is that information correct, if so, how many of such claims were settled, and had these claims reference to the pieces or sections of land that the hon. member for Carleton referred to?
The hon. member must be referring to the Canadian Northern Railway system?
Yes.
I have no information in connection with that. I never heard of the matter before.
I understood the minister to say there were something like 1,200 participating in the Provident fund.
I said there were 1,096. But 398 have died.

The Provident fund has been in force since 1906 or 1907. At that time it was an experiment. This fund was arranged by the then Minister of Railways and Canals and quite a large number of employees of the lower-paid classes went into that fund, their participation entitling them to the minimum amount of $20 a month. There are quite a number of these men living in Moncton and I know a number who have absolutely nothing to live upon except this $20 a month. They are in destitute circumstances, after they have given their lives, to work on the Intercolonial. We must not forget that the wages paid to these men were very much smaller than those paid to-day and notwithstanding the greatly increased cost of living they have only this small monthly allowance and they have to pay the same for whatever they purchase as the men who are working on the road and receiving higher wages. I wrote a letter to the minister in the early part of the session and I trust that the department will enter into negotiations by which fair treatment may be meted out to this class of retired Intercolonial employees. It is ridiculous to expect men, living in a city and some of them with families and without any other income, to live on the pittance that they receive from the Provident fund.

The contribution is made half by the Government and half by the employees and the Provident fund is administered by a committee composed of employees and some of the officials of the Railway Department. The whole matter was brought to my attention by my hon. friend (Mr. Copp) and I think also by one or two of the employees who were superannuated under that fund and who asked me to take the matter up. The Compensation Act has gone through this session, and it is necessary that we should take up this whole matter of the Provident fund in connection with it. It is being looked into, and as soon as the session is over, and I can get an opportunity, I intend to go into the whole matter. The point which the hon. gentleman has mentioned will have to be brought before this committee to see if something cannot be done for the old employees. I realize that their pension is very small and that something should be done. I had a gentleman to-day appealing for a larger retiring allowance. He has a pension of $20 a month, he is 80 years of age and he was on the road for forty years. But, it is not within the power of the minister to deal with the matter; the committee must agree to any changes.

The trouble is that the matter has been taken up in a half-hearted way by some members of the Provident fund board, but- there has been no one to take hold of it actively, meet the men, consider the case. I would suggest that the minister give it to some particular man in his department as part of his work, and let him look into the matter, visit the different localities and see if some scheme cannot be evolved by which fair treatment can be given both to the railway and to the men.
I think the minister said that the Government contribute $100,-

000 to the Provident fund and that it has been a fixed sum for a number of years.
Mr. J. D. -REID: That is right.
Mr. FIElLD/IN'G: If the principle of making such a grant is a sound one-and I think, on the whole it is, although I have some reason to believe that there is a difference of opinion on that-it seems to me that the grant should bear some proportion to the number of employees. The idea that there should be a fixed sum given for a .smaller number of employees and no larger sum when the number of employees has increased, does not seem to me to be consistent with sound business. There may be room for doubt as to whether or not this is the best form of dealing with the problem, but I think the sum to be contributed ought to bear some proportion to the number of employees and the contributions of the men.
Mr. J. D. REIlD: When the scheme was started the contributions, by the Government and the employees, were to be on a fifty-fifty basis. The Government's .contribution did not start with $100,000 but it was limited to $100,000, and it has reached that amount. Now that the Compensation Act has been passed, the matter will likely be taken up and some change will probably have to be made in the whole organization.

Will the House be put in possession of the whole history of this Provident fund scheme and will hon. members have an opportunity of .studying the question, not only from the viewpoint of those having it in charge but also from the purely business standpoint; and will they .have an opportunity of fully discussing it before any definite policy is laid down?

I want to make a few brief observations concerning the Prince Edward Island railway before the session is too far advanced. I am quite aware that the veteran members of Parliament know the history of that railway, but this is a new Parliament, and the new members may not be quite so well informed. To review the whole history of that railway would be too long a story to relate to-night when we are so anxious to close Parliament and return to our homes. I shall, therefore, not discuss the history of the building of the railroad in Prince Edward Island, which was one of the greatest political conspiracies ever carried out in the civilized world-a conspiracy which cost the province of Prince Edward Island its liberties, .and which robbed .the people of that province of their birthright for a mess of pottage. I am simply making the present statement as an introduction, to the speech which I propose to deliver next year if I live to return, and you will give me the hearing such as you have always accorded. First of all, let me draw the attention of the committee to the fact that Prince Edward Island paid for its own railroad. The Dominion Government does not own the Prince Edward Island railway; it holds it. in trust for the benefit of the general public. However, I am not going to enter upon a discussion of this truth to-night, because some of us are in too big a hurry to get away to Europe. All that will come up next year.
May I ask a question?
Yes, if the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Read) consents.
The hon. gentleman can ask his question.
I suggest that if Prince Edward Island owns the railway it would be a very proper thing for this House to hand it back to that province.
That is not a question.
That's a conclusion.

The Government would
never take it back and pay us what they owe us through Confederation. The present deficit on, the Prince Ediward Island railway represents the interest on the money that belonged to Prince1 Edward Island when it entered Confederation. Those of you who have studied the history of Confederation know that when the four original provinces of the Dominion-'Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick- united, they did so on the principle of funding the whole of their public debt and then crediting it on a per capita basis to be held as part of the funded debt of Canada on which they would pay five per cent per annum for all time to come. When Prince Edward Island entered the union our proportion was one-fortieth. The public debt of the four big provinces was $240,000,000 and one-fortieth of that would be $6,000,000 due to the province of Prince Edward Island, provided it had any public debt. But as a matter of fact it did not have any such obligation except the railway debt. That was imposed upon us by the connivance of the Imperial and Dominion Governments,, and the set of politicians that sold, as I have already told you, our birthright for a mess of pottage. I want the House to be seized of the fact that the money which is absorbed by the present deficit on the Prince Edward Island railway really belongs to that province. That deficit amounts this year to about $470,000. Why is that debt so great? There is no part of 'Canada which yields so, much traffic to its railway as Prince Edward Island. In the name of goodness then, why should there be a deficit? I will tell you why. I have received a letter from home to-day, a business letter, and1 the complaint made in that letter-and the complaint which has been made for the last twelve months by every business man in Prince Edward Island is that they cannot get t-heir produce carried away, they cannot get sufficient cars for the purpose and the Minister of Railways knows that. HoweveT, I am not blaming the Government for it, because, as the minister has pointed out, they intend to, widen the gauge, and they do not want to expend a considerable sum of money on, a system that is going out of use. But I am still hoping that the minister will bring down, Supplementary Estimates before the present session closes that will make provision for widening the gauge between Port Borden, Summerside and Charlottetown, and consequently obviating

the present great necessity that exists for cars and locomotives. The Government has had Dr. Robertson in Prince Edward Island telling the people to increase their production, and they are going to produce more. But what are they 'going to do with the food that is produced i,f no provision is, made for transporting it to the markets, of the mainland? That is the condition of things which exists- there to-day. Hon. gentlemen who are in the habit of reading the newspapers -will have noticed that the Food Controller has been advising the people of Peterborough, Ontario, to sell their potatoes instead of feeding them, giving, as the reason that the Prince Edward Island people are feeding their potatoes to hogs because they had not- the necessary transportation facilities to move them. The Minister of Railways has pointed out that it will take $2,000,000 to widen the gauge of the whole of the Prince Edward Island railway, with its 275 miles. But we are not asking him to undertake that work this summer. We are only urging him, between now and next September or October, to widen the gauge for a distance of sixty miles, and the bulk of that is over level country, with easy grades and bridges .already constructed.

Between, PoTt Borden and Summerside and Charlottetown. The name "Port Borden" was bestowed in recognition of the leader of the Government because he was good enough to inaugurate the car ferry system, for which we are much oj^iged to him and to the Government. There are some 49 miles between Summer-side and Charlottetown, and then there is a branch that runs down to the car ferry from Emerald Junction, some 11 miles. If we had the railway in such a shape that between now and next September or October we could use the wide gauge cars over the 60 miles referred to, it would obviate the necessity of purchasing any more narrow gauge cars or engines beyond the three or four that have been already ordered. I am not criticising the Government for the purchase of these narrow-gauge locomotives; it had to be done unless we were to go into the cellar altogether.

The Government could not
run the new private car on the narrow gauge system.

I hope the Minister of Railways -and the Government will consider our position and endeavour to make some provision for meeting our necessities during the coming summer. I asik this House to be fair to our little province, for we have been the "staggering bob" on the Dominion for -many years.
Sir Richard Cartwright used to claim that Ontario was Canada's milch cow. We are the " staggering bob," the poor little sister bled white, though not by any intention on the part of the big provinces, who have not understood our situation. When we , went into Confederation the Government put in the terms certain statutory promise; -or, rather, not promises merely, but statutory contracts. And one of them was that we were to have uninterrupted steam communication, summer and winter, so as to connect the Prince Edward Island railway with the railroad system of the Dominion. After forty-five years of waiting this contract was only fulfilled last October. I am proud to think that the Government has found a way to overcome the difficulties. All governments have made an honest endeavour at one time and another to give us winter communication, and have provided -the Stanley, the Minto, the Earl Grey and all those beautiful ships. But they could not do the trick. Now they have a vessel that can. All I am pleading for now is that the Government will take into consideration the situation in-our province and appropriate at least $300,000 or $400.000 to widen the gauge on the sections of the line I have referred to. I believe It will cost only $2,000,000 to standardize the gauges on the whole line, and the $400,000 I am asking for is a mere bagatelle in these days when we are talking hundreds nf millions.

I am pleased to notice that the Minister of Railways has an item of $65,000 in his estimates fbr the completion of the terminals at Port Borden and Cape Tormentine, where the car ferry steamer Prince Edward' Island plies between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. I need not say that I deeply regret that the minister has not found it convenient to include an amount in the estimates, at least to commence the standardization of the gauge on the Prince Edward Island railway. I would not suggest to the Government, as my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Read) has done, to standardize the gauge from Port Borden to Summer-side and from Port Borden to Charlottetown. That would only be a piece-meal pro-

posal. I would not dictate or suggest to the Government where they should begin. But I sincerely desire that they shall make a beginning -as soon as . reasonably possible. And when they do begin to standardize, it should be done in such a way that all portions of the province traversed by the railway will be benefited. As I had occasion to say before, in consequence of the dearth of coastal steamships, the removal of the products of Prince Edward Island will be a very difficult problem this very year. Notwithstanding that a great many of our sons, I am proud to say, have gone to fight our battles at the front, I am satisfied that there will be a very considerable increase of agricultural production in Prince Edward Island this year. That being so, we shall have much more to export to provide food for the soldiers fighting our battles. We have scarcely any idea of how productive Prince Edward Island is, for the very fact that we have never had sufficient facilities to ship our products from the Island. The car ferry steamer "Prince Edward Island" is a splendid ship. In my opinion, she is the greatest product of marine architecture of her class. During the past winter, which was unprecedently severe and arduous, she made daily trips across the Straits; several times a day, sometimes. As I said before, the question of winter navigation of the Straits has been solved. The * solution of that problem, which had caused so much difficulty, hardship, disappointment and uncertainty to our people, has caused a revolution of feeling, and the matter of winter navigation of the straits is now accepted as beyond any question. Consequently we feel exceedingly grateful to the Government for what they have done in furnishing this magnificent steamer, and solving this difficult problem, and placing us in continuous communication with the Intercolonial and other railway systems of the Dominion, which was written in the bond at the time we entered Confederation. It was the lack of this understanding which prevented Prince Edward Island from going into Confederation with the original four provinces in 1867. In 1873 the Imperial Order in Council contained what the Island asked for, -but it is only now that we have succeeded in gettiqg the link across the Straits. As the minister knows, the standardization of the gauge is the complement of the ear ferry -steamer. I think I can thus speak, though I have no warrant for it:	As we all know, the people of Prince
Edward Island are not poor, although it is a small place. They have, contributed most

generously to the loans that Canada has floated. I feel I am safe in saying that if the Government would issue a special loan of $2,000,000 for the purpose of broadening the gauge on the Prince Edward Island railway, . the people of Prince Edward Island have the money; and they would buy the bonds and furnish the necessary funds to complete the work. If the Government take that departure, they will solve at least one difficulty in connection with the problem of standardizing the road. If the Minister of Railways, in his supplementary estimates, provides a sum for the commencement of this work he will do something that will be dear to the hearts of the people of Prince Edward Island, something for which the people of tha-t province will never cease to be thankful, and something which will be a benefit to the whale Dominion as well.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the matter of the acquirement by the Government of the Caraquet and Gulf Shore Railway in Gloucester county. I hold no brief for the company which operates that road; my brief is for the people of Gloucester county. Indeed, this is a national as well as a local question; it affects not only the interests of my county, but the larger interests of the Dominion. During the last two months the Minister of Railways has received many petitions on behalf of th: people of Gloucester county requesting that the Government take over that road. I do not wish to 6ay anything in disparagement of the company which operates that road, but if I point out that through lack of initiative, of wise administration, or if ability to raise the necessary capital the road is in an embarrassed condition and the people of Gloucester cour.ty are thereby suffering inconveniences in the matter of transportation of their products to the markets which are clamouring for them, I do so only in order to put the case as it is before the Government. I wish to read only one of the many petitions which have been sent, as indicating the gravity of the situation to-day in that distrief^the most potential district in the matter of resources not, only in New Brunswick, but, considering its size, in the whole of Canada.
Caraquet, N.-B., March 22, 1918. O. Turgeon, M.P.,	.
Ottawa, Ont.
At a public meeting held here last night the following resolutions were unanimously passed :
Whereas petitions pointing out the dilapidated and unsafe condition of the Caraquet and Gulf Shore railway and its unfitness to satisfactorily perform the public service required of it were
signed 'by a large number of the residents and ratepayers of this county, and forwarded to the Hon. P. B. Carvell, Minister of Public Works, Ottawa, respectfully asking that the Government acquire the railway and "operate it as part of the Government railway system in the interest of the people; and, whereas the Caraquet and Gulf Shore railway represents the only system of transportation on the south side of bay Chaleur from Bathurst to Shippigan and Tra-cadie, a distance of more than hundred miles on which is dependent the traffic resulting from the agriculture, lumbering and extensive fishing industries along the coast; and whereas the service performed by the railway, which for some time has been most unsatisfactory and irregular, has become entirely inadequate to handle the increased traffic, notwithstanding the equipment recently obtained from the Government; and whereas the Government has taken no definite action thus far to acquire the railway and operate it in the interests of the people;	.
Therefore resolved, that in the opinion of this meeting, representative of the industrial, agricultural and fishing interests of the community, the time has now arrived when serious loss and injury will occur to these industries unless the railway is taken over by the Government at as early a date as possible and operated as part of the Government railway system.

The minister has received many such petitions from residents of the districts traversed by that railway. Since I first became a member of this House it has been my duty on many occasions, on behalf of my constituents, to request that this road, which for some reason has never been operated as it should have been in the public interest, be taken over by the Government and operated as part of the Canadian Government railways. The main line of the Government road passes through the head of the Gloucester peninsula. Sir Sanford Fleming had a survey .made m 1873 and 1874, and it was his plan at that time to construct a branch line in that county as part of the Government road. Had this proposal been accepted, direct communication with Newfoundland would have been afforded and Newfoundland would have undoubtedly entered the Confederation. It was understood by the people of Canada that the construction of branch lines in that county as well as on the other side of 'Chaleur bay should not be left to private enterprise, because a branch line cannot be expected to pay unless it belongs to the company holding the trunk line. The Government made a great mistake when they allowed this branch line railway in Gloucester county to be constructed by private enterprise. However, a few men were trying to get sufficient capital together in order to build branch lines, and they got-

a charter for the construction of this road. As far back as 1882, as an independent candidate I was advocating the construction of that line by the Government. My Conservative opponent, a man of wealth, advocated the construction of the line by a private company under subsidy. He got ' the subsidy and built the road-and died from worry. Although, that line is in a dilapidated condition, if the minister acquires it he will not be getting a road which has no value. If it has not great worth as a road, owing to its condition, it has great value because of the potentialities of the district through which it runs. 'It is not a line of railway ten or fifteen *miles in length, a distance over which traffic might to-day be readily carried on *by auto-trucks; it is 88J miles long, and serves one of the richest districts of northern New Brunswick with its wealth of resources of land and sea. A few years ago that industry . was not of much value to the road, because the price of lumber was low, and the lumber cut along that road could be transported by water. To-day there is no more transportation by water, while there is at present an immense demand for lumber in the American market, and it commands a high price. There is no limit to the thousands of cars of lumber the district [DOT]along this road can produce. Before the minister answers my hon. friend I should like to ask whether he has received a petition from the inhabitants of the town, of Sioux Lookout requesting that the name of the railway station 'be changed to the name of their town. The matter might have the appearance of having politics in it, but I can assure the minister that there are none. The name of Sioux Lookout is an old name that wae given to the place long before the
railway went through. It is the junction point of the waters by which the Indians from lake Superior used to travel westwards, and the Sioux on a high hill could see them coming a long way off, and so the town got its name, just as Medicine Hat got its name. When the railway was built, the place began to grow and eventually became a divisional point. The station wae then called Graham. But the town, name is still Sioux Lookout; the post office is Sioux Lookout; the registry office plan is under the name of iSioux Lookout, and if you wish to write a letter to a person there you have to address* it Sioux Lookout; but if you want to send a telegram it has to be addressed, to Graham, and it is exceedingly confusing. It would be a pity to see the name of Graham disappear from the Transcontinental, but one of the other divisional points east or west, Armstrong or Redditt, for instance, might take that name, or if it was desired to give the name to a junction point, why not call Superior Junction, where the railway comes down to lake Superior, Graham? But to continue the name of Graham for the railway station and Sioux Lookout for the post office is certainly confusing to business life. The people will not give up their name of Sioux Lookout, all their deeds and conveyances being under that name in the registry office plan, and that being vlso the name of the post office. I should like to know whether they have asked the minister to change the name, and whether he can see his way clear to do so, giving the name of Graham to some other divisional point.

I have received petitions and numerous requests to change the name of the station. The petitioners if I remember rightly, stated that Sioux Lookout was the name of the town, an incorporated town, I believe, and the post office and registry office was also in that name. Every reason appeared in the petition why the name of the railway station should be changed to Sioux Lookout, but I will frankly admit that I have hesitated to change the name of the station because it was named after the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals. He had a great deal to do with the building of this railway. He lives within a few miles of me, and we have always, been friends, and I have hesitated, and hesitate now, to change the name for that reason, because- it might be thought that since I had become Minister of Railways I had some other object in-changing the name.
Why not name one of the other divisional points Graham?

I believe that if the minister takes over any of these branch lines he will find that the Caraquet and Gulf Shore traverses a district having the greatest potentialities and from which he will in future get a more profitable traffic than from any other part of the country. None of these roads travels through a .wealthier district than that traversed by the Caraquet and Gulf Shore. If he once gets possession of that line he will find its operation profitable. It is for that reason that- we are so anxious to have it transferred from the company to the Government. The minister tells me that he has made an offer equal to that which he has made to the other companies in New Brunswick and that while the others have accepted offers made to them, this company has not accepted. I do not wish to say that the minister has not offered enough. I am not an engineer and I wdll not put my estimate upon the railway itself. I can indicate the value of the road better by estimating the traffic that is to come to it in the future than I can by putting any value on the road itself. Meanwhile I would say that perhaps if he were to put. in his Estimates the price which he offers the owners of the road might be disposed, or induced, to accept it.
I could not do that.
Then why not leave it to arbitration?
No; if they do not take it now I will not put it in.
The minister is willing to pay the price that he says he has offered the company. The company ask for a little more.
The company ask double what I offered them.

Even if it is double, let it be referred to arbitration and it is most likely that the decision trill be on the side of the Government. If the minister is willing to spend so much for bridges, repairs and so on to put it in good condition, is it worth while, for the sake of a few thousand dollars, separating the county of Gloucester from the rest- of the Dominion?
They are not anxious to sell and I am not anxious to buy.

The minister may not be anxious to buy but in the exercise of his duty he should consider the interests of the north shore of New Brunswick as well as the interests of any other portion of the country. It is well known that in 1911 the Government of that day, at my insistent request and at the request of other members from New Brunswick, gave some attention to this question. I see my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) coming into the House and I am very glad. I missed him during my first remarks. I wall ask him to corroborate the statements I have made in his absence. I was asking if it was worth while, for the sake of a few thousand dollars, to differentiate from the rest of the country the county of Gloucester or the northern part of New Brunswick whose advantages, from the railway point of view, will, <in the future, exceed those of any other district. I stated that the Caraquet and Gulf Shore railway traversed an immense district in the eastern portion of Gloucester which is the wealthiest district in New Brunswick to-day.. Railway traffic is assured in the abundance of those products which are the most profitable in the operation of a railway, more particularly the lumber traffic. The lumber traffic is certainly one out of which the railways can make more money than they can out of any other kind of business.
This railway traverses a district, as I have already said, where there is as yet virgin

forest, and; where the great industry of agriculture has been progressing rapidly, more particularly for the last few years. As .the Minister of Public Works knows, that railway, starting from Bathurst runs for a distance of 20 or 25 miles through a long-settled agricultural district inhabited by an active and enterprising population who have progressed in agriculture for the last forty years. The salmon fishing industry needs prompt railway transportation in order that its yield may be placed on the market as rapidly as possible. It is now separated from the main station at Bathurst by distances extending anywhere from ten, fifteen, twenty and thirty-five miles. The Minister of Public Works knows of the operations that are- going on at Stone Haven where there is a <quarry with one hundred carloads of stone ready to be transported to the province of Ontario, and which could easily double and treble its output if there was only certainty of getting those transportation facilities which have been lacking. At Caraquet there, is the great fishing industry requiring the services of 256 schooners daily, and with a catch of fish easily estimated at $1,000,000 a year. No one can over-estimate the importance of this industry in helping to feed our soldiers at the front. Then there is the great lumbering industry, between Caraquet, Burnsville and Tracadie, which also is in need of proper transportation facilities. The Minister of Public Works knows that there are vast forest areas which are capable of supplying millions of tons of pulp-wood to the industry at Bathurst, which has furnished a large amount of traffic for the last five or six years in that district. He knows the increased prices which the pulp company has had to pay owing to the condition of the railway, and that it has thousands of cords of pulpwood lying alongside the line which cannot at present be transported because the freight charges are too high. He knows that every statement that I am making on this subject to-night is correct, and he knows the potentialities of that district just as well as I do. He cannot say that I am exaggerating	at all	the possibilities of the	district of	which
I am. speaking. If, in the Prairie Provinces there was a stretch of eighty-eight miles in which a good railroad service hud Ibeen lacking during the last twenty or thirty years, so that the development of the district was retarded, the farmers would long ago have insisted on the Government taking over that line and giving them a proper service for the carriage of their wheat.

If to-day the branch lines in New Brunswick are in a dilapidated condition, successive Governments of Canada in the past which allowed these companies to build the small branch lines are responsible for it, and during the past few years the people living in the districts through which they pass have Ibeen encouraged to hope that the Government would take these roads over. In 1911 the late Goveftiment introduced a Bill which passed its first reading and was awaiting the return of Parliament to undergo its second reading, providing for taking over the road of which I have been speaking, together with others. During that election the present Prime Minister, at the request of his supporters in New Brunswick, wired to Mr. Fowler, now a member of the Upper Chamber, who was at that time a candidate in Kings county, declaring that if his party were returned to power he would not depart from the Liberal policy in regard to the acquisition of branch lines in New Brunswick, but that his .administration would also take over these branch lines.

That was an election promise, and it has not been carried out. During the last two or three years I have constantly urged this, matter on. the Minister of Railways, amd have received the reply that owing to war conditions it was impossible to get the necessary money to take over these lines. I would like to say that the advent of the present Government preceded the outbreak of war. There was a period of three years before the war during which opportunity was afforded of carrying out its promise. Let me say that the conditions last winter on these branch lines were almost intolerable. It is hard enough in the case of passengers, but where freight is concerned it is almost impossible to secure any transportation. I would urge the Government, in view of the fact that it has decided to take over branch lines elsewhere,, to see whether it cannot do something for New Brunswick, even if it involves some sacrifice.
