stated. With his statement of facts that the condition of affairs which has existed with respect to the branch lines in the province of New Brunswick has become almost unbearable, I have very little quarrel indeed. Twenty-five or thirty years ago, when railway construction in Eastern Canada was fairly in its infancy, when railway communication was beginning to be called for, and the Government of the day refused to build branch lines, the people organized small companies and built them themselves.
The Intercolonial through New Brunswick, as you will observe by looking at the map, does not follow the seacoast where the settlements are, but runs some twenty-five or thirty miles away. Unfortunately, a very great portion of the central part of New Brunswick on the eastern side is not very valuable land. But along the seacoast it is valuable land, .and there is a very dense population, the descendants of the old French settlers who came there a hundred and fifty years ago or more. It became necessary then to -build branch lines from the main line running down to the seaboard and the Bay of Fundy, as well as on Northumberland strait and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. There were six of these roads altogether. There is another small road, built from Cross- Creek, on what is now a portion of the Government railways, to the town of Stanley, in the county of York, but it is not of the same class as the six roads I have referred to. These road's all received *small subsidies, probably $6,000 a mile would be the maximum amount of assistance, and in many cases much less than that. In some cases they got a Dominion subsidy of $3,200 a mile and $2,500 a mile from the province of New Brunswick. For. a number of years after their construction they got along very well, until the time of replacement arrived. They had no reserves, and were not in a position to charge sufficient rates; in fact, there was not sufficient traffic to justify them in keeping the roads up to standard and they commenced to deteriorate. The result was that about ten or fifteen years ago, or a little before that period, practically all these roads went under the hammer; they were foreclosed by the bondholders and bid in by certain parties. Many of the owners of these roads have fairly large amounts of money invested in them-I know-as my bon. friend (Mr. Turgeon) s-ays regarding the road in his constituency, that the Oara-quet railway has cost the present owners quite a large amount of money; I don't know how much. We had several representatives before us
a few days ago, who said they could not tell us what it did cost. However, there is no doubt that the roads cost a great deal more money than the Government is offering for them. When the late Hon. Mr. Emmerson was Minister of Railways and canals a very strong agitation sprang up to have these roads taken over by the Intercolonial, as it was then called. I have *always supported that proposition, and I am on record a great many times in this House during the last fifteen years as advocating the acquisition of all branch lines by the trunk line, for the simple reason that under modem conditions it is impossible to operate branch lines successfully. I do not believe there is a place in Canada in which a branch line could he economically operated. It must become part of the main trunk line. That policy has been laid down by the Grand Trunk, the iGrand Trunk 'Pacific, and the Canadian Northern, and by the Government railways to quite an extent. Unfortunately, however, the acquisition of these roads from the very beginning of the agitation down to a few months ago was simply used as a. .political football. Not an election, *either provincial or federal, 'has been run in the province of New Brunswick in the last ten or twelve years, I am safe in saying in which the question of the acquisition of these lines has not been an issue, and both parties have used it as a football for political benefit. I do not think I am going too far when I say that some of the gentlemen who purchased these roads did -so with the idea of selling them to the Government. I do know that when an attempt was made within the last five years to take over some of these roads, there was always the inevitable grafter who had to have his thirty-three and a third ,per cent. But the -Government .would not pay that and I give them all credit for not doing so.
When I became Minister of Public Wotks, last October, the representative of practically every one of these roads came to me to exact a promise that these roads would be taken over, and I absolutely refused to have anything to do with it or to make any promise whatever. I told them I would not be a party to holding out the purchase of these lines as an election promise, hut that I would see that they were operated during the coming winter, because I believed that was necessary. 1 discussed the matter with my colleague the Minister of Railways, and an Order in Council was passed giving the Govern-

ment railways the right to operate these roads and supply whatever was necessary in the way of equipment, men, and even money, on the principle that the roads must be kept open. Probably it was the worst winter for railroading we have had in the Maritime Provinces for the past twenty years. But, through the activities of the railroads themselves, assisted by the Government railways, they were kept open with very few intervals. There may have been a week or two when one or another was closed down. After the election was over I asked my colleagues to adopt the policy of purchasing these branch lines, and I do not think I am revealing any confidence when I say that it took a great deal of persuasion on my part to bring them to consent to it. However, they agreed, and the Minister of Railways and myself were appointed a committee to purchase them under certain restrictions. Now, Mr. Chairman, we were bound to approach the question of the purchase of these lines, not from the standpoint of what the people had put into them, not to consider any set of men who were losing or making money, but on the principle of what the Government could afford to give. I have no hesitation in saying that they did not put back into these roads anything like what would be required by ordinary railroad management in the way of replacement. The roads had gone down in their physical condition until they were the veritable "one hoss shay"; they were ready to fall to pieces. Yet the people who owned these roads, or their predecessors, had put into them very large amounts of money. We were obliged to approach the purchase of these roads more from the standpoint of necessary accommodation to the people who lived in the locality, and anything which we offer to the owners of these roads is more in the way of a bonus for the purpose of giving accommodation to the people than as a purchase price for the railways themselves. I hope there will not be any misunderstanding as to the principle on which we approached the purchase of these roads. I admit that the amount of $2,000 a mile, which is probably the average price offered, is ridiculous when you consider what the roads have cost. I admit that every -one of these companies, could tear up their rails and sell them for two or three times what we are willing to pay for the roads as they stand. I believe my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) is right. However, it is a fact that they could take up the rails at the present price of steel and get-	,
Double.

Yes. But we admit at once that we are not purchasing these roads from the standpoint of what they cost at all. If men in the United States and Canada have been unfortunate enough to put their money into an unprofitable venture, that is their misfortune and not ours, and we cannot under any consideration whatever attempt to reimburse these people because of their unbusinesslike venture.
We have offered these companies virtually $2,000 a mile-really only a bonus to get rid of them, and to provide that the people living along these lines may have the necessary accommodation. I think I am safe in saying that within the next two years the Government will have to spend another $2,000 a mile to make these roads passable. But the Government can operate them very much better than local companies can, because large quantities of second-hand and light equipment, both motive power and cars, which are not fit for use on the main lines, can be used on these branch lines. These small roads have practically no rolling stock. They have engines of an obsolete character, but they have practically no cars. Shippers along these lines cannot get the accommodation to which they are entitled because they cannot get cars. Naturally, the Canadian Government Railway authorities supply their own shippers with cars before they devote their attention to outsiders, and the result is that the industrial life of the northern and eastern portions of New Brunswick have been absolutely stagnant for the last ten years because of the lack of railway facilities. 1 make no apology, even under present financial conditions, for the policy which I have asked my colleagues to adopt in connection with these roads. Wg have entered into agreement to purchase four of these roads, and the matter will- be submitted to the House for consideration in the form of supplementary estimates. The prices vary, but they average $2,000 a mile. The price offered for .some is a little less than that; in one case, because the road was in very much worse physical condition than the others. In two cases, I think, the price slightly exceeds $2,000 a mile; in one of these cases the road is very much better equipped with rolling stock and motive power than the others. One has 67-pound rails, practically new, which will last for the next fifty years; the others have 52 and 56-pound rails. We took these things into consideration to some extent, but not wholly, because if we had regard to the value of t\ie rails as they are to-day for

junk, we should have to pay twice as much as we are offering. We have bought three of the roads running from the main line of the Intercolonial to the sea. We have bought a fourth running from Cross Creek to Stanley in the county of York, which is not in the same category as the others; it is simply a small branch line. Then there are three others, two in Kent-the Moncton and Buctouche and the Kent Northern.-and the Caraquet Railway referred to by the member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon). I admit, that we have offered to the owners of the Caraquet Railway an amount which is probably less than the road cost them. But the difficulty is that the Caraquet Railway to-day is practically impossible of operation; at least $2,000 or $3,000 a mile will have to be expended on the road in order to make possible the running of a freight train over it, let alone a passenger train. We are therefore compelled to approach this subject from the standpoint not of what the road cost, but of what is the lowest amount of money which will give the 25,000 or 30,000 people in that portion of New Brunswick the railway communication to which they are entitled. Although the amount which we have offered is practically in the form of a bonus, it is really more than the Gov' ernment ought to offer, from a strict business standpoint. The member for Gloucester has given this matter more consideration, probably, than any member of the House, during the last ten or twelve years, and he is entitled to my views on the subject. I have certainly been very frank with him. I hope that the owners of the road running through his good county will see their way clear to accept our terms. Not one of these roads has made a dollar during the last ten years, if you take into consideration the amount necessary for replacements. They have made a little money-from $1,000 to $5,000 a year-but they have made it only by starving the roads and putting them in such a condition that they are now practically impassable. The question for these gentlemen to consider is whether they will hang on to a venture in which they have put a good deal of money and from which they get no revenue, or whether they will transfer them to the Government for a very small amount of cash from which they can get a revenue. Of course, if they will not take what we offer them, we will not buy. But we shall have to adopt some measure to keep these roads going. As long as I remain in this Government, those roads are going to run, in prder that the people in that part of
the province may get proper railway communication. If we cannot deal with these gentlemen in one way, we will deal with them in another. In any case, we are not going to make them a present of a large amount of money.
Very strong powers are conferred under the War Measures Act. Anyway, I repeat, these roads shall run, and we will not pay the fancy prices they want for them, either.

My bon. friend, therefore, may feel assured that no discrimination has been exercised against the railway in his county. I can go further and say that none of the seven roads is in as deplorable a state physically as the Caraquet railway.

I understand that the minister does not desire to discriminate. The Prime Minister pointed out only yesterday that when it came to acquiring and determining the value of large railway systems in which enormous amounts of money have been invested, arbitration was the best solution. This principle applies to small

lines as well as the 'big ones, to a matter of
11,000	as well as to a matter of $1,000,000. The Department of Railways, in the interest of the people, should expropriate the road. I remember a commission was some years ago sent down to the Maritime Provinces to investigate which lines should be acquired as feeders for the Intercolonial as being paying concerns for the road. If I am not mistaken, the Temiscouata railway was one of the best paying roads, and it should have been acquired at the time.
I do not know why it has not been purchased. The farmers along that road are at present obliged to pay very high rates for transportation, and if the road was acquired by the Intercolonial, the people along the road would be benefited as well as the Intercolonial itself. I want to ask the Minister of Railways why that road was not 'acquired. 'He has in contemplation the purchase of branch lines which are not paying propositions. It is true the acquisition of those roads will be of benefit for the people, but they will mean an expense to the Intercolonial. On the other hand, the acquisition of the Temiscouata railway will be a paying concern as a feeder for the Intercolonial.
I wish to draw the minister's attention to a little! matter in connection with the Intercolonial which is causing annoyance. With reference to the purchase of the Temiscouata Railway, the hon. member says that that railway is kept in good condition and operated successfully, and that the people in that locality are well served by the road. I am not going around trying to buy railways. The trouble is that these railways that we are -taking over are in such a condition that they cannot operate, they must close down unless assistance is given. We were compelled, therefore, a-s I stated a few minutes ago, to pass an Order in Council authorizing -the Canadian Government Railways to operate them on their behalf.

Those railways are really going to close down unless something is done, and that is the reason why we are compelled to take them over. As the Temiscouata Railway is being operated' successfully in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, we are quite satisfied that the company should continue to operate the road and make money out of it. If it is a paying road, the shareholders will not want to part with it.
What about the farmers?

The farmers, as the hon. member states, are well served by the road, and so far as the rates are concerned, I suppose the Temiscouata railway is under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and, therefore, no exorbitant rates can be charged. My hon. friend probably feels that rates are lower on the Intercolonial. I think the rates are about the same on the Intercolonial as on other roads. If not, they should be, and so far as rates and protection from fire service on the Intercolonial are concerned, we are in about the same position as the other railways, and during this war we do not want to buy the Temiscouata Railway or any other road if they can operate without assistance from the Government.

I did not notice in the statement made by the minister any reference to the number of accidents and collisions on the Government railways, and the loss of life and the damage to property thereby occasioned, during the last year's operations.
I have not those figures with me, but I could have them here when the Supplementary Estimates are up.

I think it would be well
to have statistical information in regard to those matters. Referring to the minister's statement, I presume that in "construction betterments " includes improvements to station houses, railway yards, and things of that kind. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, replying to the hon. m'ember for Gloucester, told us that he made a promise to the electors of New Brunswick during the last election that the branch lines would be operated last winter. I do not know how fully he has implemented that promise, but I do know that a number of the branch lines were not in operation throughout the winter, and I presume my hon. friend the *member for St. John, who during the election campaign was forced to drive from
(Moncton to the county of Albert, will agree *that the line running into part of his constituency was not very much in operation during that period. I am not blaming the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Railways, but I should like to have the minister assure us that the main line of *the Intercolonial at least will be kept in [DOT]operation next winter. It certainly was not kept in operation last winter, and I presume the Minister of Railways will say that that was because they were short of motive power.
We had all the motive power we wanted.

If that is so, the minister
did not make a very great success of the operation of the road last winter. Of course it may have been impossible to do any better. I am not a railway expert, but I know that the conditions in our part of the province of New Brunswick were very unsatisfactory indeed. So much by way of general criticism.
Now I wish to call the minister's attention to what is. going on at Sackville, which is the junction point of the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway that was recently taken over by the Government. That road was in bad condition when it was taken over, to connect up with Cap Tormentine and the car ferry running to Prince Edward Island, but improvements, which were very much needed, have since been made in order to handle the freight between Sackville and Cap Tormentine over this thirty-six miles of road. When communication was established last fall, the Railway Department was not in a position to handle the traffic. I suppose it did not realize how great the volume of that traffic was going to be. As my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island said, it perhaps little knew the great productivity of the province at the other end of the car ferry. At all events, the road was simply overwhelmed with traffic, and there was no place to put the freight cars. Passenger trains were held up for an hour at a time because the main line was blocked with freight cars. I am not complaining, because as I have said, no doubt the officials of the railway did not realize the amount of traffic that would come over the line. What I do complain of is that now, when preparations are being made for that traffic, when new sidings and roundhouses are being constructed, exactly the same thing is being done in the town of Sackville as occurred in the city of Moncton. The terminal facilities that are being provided are

not one-quarter the size they should be to handle the traffic that will develop in a very short time. To-day, shunting engines and trains are holding up traffic in the principal streets of the town of Sackville. It is a nuisance already, and the Board of trade and the town council of Sackville are taking steps to remove the nuisance. The work that is being done there now will have to be thrown away in a few years, and new arrangements made for the traffic to go overhead or by subway. I tell the minister that his officials are only half doing the job, because the traffic, instead of decreasing, will increase year by year. I would urge the minister to have this matter investigated, because I can assure him that before the snow flies next winter delegations will be waiting on him to insist that something be done to overcome this nuisance of the trains crossing the main -streets of the town of Sackville, and now is the time, before the Government has spent a large sum of money, to make adequate preparations for the traffic that will develop down there in the next two or three years.
There is another matter I wish to refer to, and I am sure the minister does not know anything about it. I was very much surprised, when I went home last week for a day or two, to find contractors already on the ground at Sackville excavating for an extension to the station house. Some seven or eight years ago the old station house was burnt down and a splendid stone building was erected in its place. Imagine my surprise the other day when I found that to provide additional accommodation the Government were excavating for a common wooden building as an extension to the beautiful stone station at Sackville. The , stone building was practically fireproof, but now the Government are going to put up a wooden building and run the risk of it burning down the whole station. That seems to me most unbusinesslike. I am told-I cannot vouch for this, but I have no doubt it is true-that the Sackville Board of Trade went to the city of Moncton and interviewed the railway authorities there, and what do you think that delegation was told? I hate to repeat it, because I cannot realize how a member of any board of trade would listen to-such a thing. The railway officials told them they were going to put up a wooden building now, and build stone around it at some other time. When I was leaving the station the other day I said to the man who was doing the excavating, " I suppose you are putting in a very solid foundation." He said, "No,

it does not require a heavy foundation, because it is only for a small building." I said: " They are going to build stone around this?" He said, " Are they? That is all you know about it." That is what is going on. It is a small matter and the minister does not know about it probably, but it does seem a ridiculous proposition to build a wooden extension to a stone building. It destroys the beauty of the surroundings and' I doubt if it will not cost more to build it with wood than to continue it with stone.
I know nothing about the situation. I have never been in Sackville.
Come down with me when I go home.

I shall make inquiries as to what they are doing there. I have not had an opportunity of going over the Intercolonial system, but as soon as the House prorogues, or within a few days afterwards, it is my intention to take a trip over the road and this is one of the things I will look into.

I am not here to represent the speculators or the branch-line owners, but I am here to represent the people who are served by these branch lines. The answers given to the questions put before the Government were not altogether satisfactory to me, with the exception of the statement made by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) that these branch lines would be operated. I understood the Government had power to force these companies to run these roads to the satisfaction of the people and of the Government. If that is the case it will be satisfactory. The people who live frotti twenty-five to one hundred miles away from the Intercolonial are certainly entitled to some consideration on the part- of the Government. I am not here to discuss politics, but I am here to discuss the interests of the people whom I represent, and who contributed their share to the building of the Intercolonial, which serves those living within a certain distance of each side of the road. But those living at a distance from the road and on. the shores, farmers and fishermen who are trying to make a living out of their industry, should have the advantage of railway transportation in order to be able to market their products to the best advantage. They have to sell their products at a lower price because of the high freight rates. If it is left in the hand's of the owners of these roads, and if nothing is

done to better the situation, I cannot see how it is going to end'. I would suggest that the Government take charge of these roads, as they have the power to take over any property that in- the public interest it may he necessary for them to acquire. If they cannot agree upon the price they have a way of taking over these roads by expropriation. Let them, then, expropriate the roads. Whether people are engaged in fishing or agriculture, we are anxious to give them every encouragement. I believe it is the duty of the Government to- take steps to serve the people throughout the country as- best they can and in such a way as to promote their interest and the public welfare generally.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to criticise the Minister of Railways for his generosity towards the branch lines in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia-
He 'has not touched Nova Scotia yet.

I have heard discussions dhirimg every session I have been in Parliament about acquiring branch lines in New Brunswick. But my hon. friend does not move very fast. He remains in the Maritime provinces and does not seem to reach *Quebec.
I started at the eastern end.	,

You are not coming on the flyer. I happen to represent, concurrently with the county of Maisonneuve, the county of Gaspe, and I consider Gaspe a9 one of the Maritime Provinces. In the beginning of the last century, Gaspe was a province by itself. It was only by the Act of 1791, if I mistake not, that Gaspe was annexed to the province of Quebec, and for a certain length of time I think it was a part of New Brunswick. I have been at Gaspe.

ministered, the trains are running regularly, and under the present management the line is paying its own expenses, but the first 100 miles would have to be practically rebuilt, and this work ought to be done by the Government. While the present war conditions prevail, I do not wish to impose on my hon. friend's shoulders an additional burden, and I do not ask the Government to take over that road now, but there is on the statute book legislation which would enable that to be done. I hope that when the war is ovier and financial conditions have improved the Government will accord that section of the country what is due to it. There are a number of thriving industries in that district. First of all, we have the fisheries, then there is the pulp industry- which is developed to a considerable degree-and of late a group of Montreal financiers, I think it is the Lyall syndicate, have been exploiting a copper mine which was discovered some few years ago between Newport and New Carlisle, and which promises to create in that locality a very prosperous mining enterprise. If the Government intends to follow up the policy of acquiring branch lines- and I do not begrudge what is (being done for New. Brunswick and for the western prairies-it should not lose sight of the fact that the peninsula of Gaspe is entitled to consideration. For, let it be remembered, it is the oldest section in the country. When Jacques Cartier ascended the river St. Lawrence he planted a cross at Gaspe at a spot which I have visited several times. So it seems to me that if we are to consider the proprieties, the oldest spot in the country should be best served. But we are not so ambitious as to press that point. Another point and I shall .have concluded.

[Mr. Lemieux.l
the French Canadian custom, in raising a large family. He was mayor of his parish, warden of the county, and had once or twice 'been offered the Conservative nomination, hut had declined because of business reasons.

No doubt about that.

Perhaps I might explain. As the law stood at the time of the fire, under the Government Railways Act, the Intercolonial was not responsible unless the fire originated on the right of way and extended to the property destroyed. About two months, I- believe, after this loss occurred, the law was changed to bring it into conformity with the general law of Canada. My hon. friend will probably remember that there was a case in Ontario between the Grand Trunk and another party whose name I have forgotten, *which went through the courts, and in which it was held that the railway company was responsible. About two months afterwards, following out the decision in that case, the law was changed so far as the Government railways were concerned. In looking over the items for public works and improvements, I find that no -amount has been provided for the works in Quebec city, although we are asked to provide many millions for works in different parts of the country. It has been said that the works in Quebec as well as other works throughout the country should not be proceeded with during the war. But surely some of the important works in Quebec city should be proceeded with. An agreement was made between the Federal Government andi the city of Quebec in August, 1910, under which the city of Quebec handed over to the Government a property valued at over $2,000,000 in connection with the works in that city. 1 submit that these works are urgent and essential, in the interest not only of the city and the province of Quebec *but of the whole of Canada as well. Large sums of money have already been spent on the terminals in Quebec for equipment of the Transcontinental and for the building of the Transcontinental shops. These shops have now been finished nearly two years, but are lying idle. Some time ago I learned with pleasure that the Government bad decided to give contracts for the supplying of 7,500 cars for the Transcontinental railway. I hoped at that time that some of these cars would be built in the Transcontinental shops at Quebec, which were designed for the purpose of doing such work. But all the contracts were given outside; nothing was provided for Quebec. The citizens of Quebec and the board of trade of that city have sent many requests to the Government in this matter during the last few years, but nothing has been done. We had the pleasure of having in our city in October, 1913, the Prime Minister and his colleagues, Mr. Cochrane, Mr. Pelletier, Mr. Rogers and Mr. Hazen, who all conceded that these works were of great importance and should be proceeded with at once. On that occasion the Prime Minister laid the cornerstone of the St. Malo shops and .of the works on the St. Charles river, and visited other important works. But all these works have been stopped and nothing is provided in the Estimates for their continuation. The city of Quebec is not asking for any favour. We aie simply asking the Government to give that portion of the country its rights and to carry out the agreement made. At least a reasonable amount should be placed in the Supplementary Estimates to carry out some of the works, to provide equipment for the Transcontinental Railway

at Quebec, to proceed with the terminal works, in order that the Transcontinental may take care of the great traffic from the West which should pass through Quebec.' It is well known that two-thirds of the grain from the West is now shipped through United States ports instead of through Quebec or other Canadian ports, because of lack of proper terminal and other Canadian ports, because of lack of proper terminal and other accommodation. I ask the Minister of Railways to look into this matter and see that justice is done to the city of Quebec.

Matters in connection with railways at Quebec will have to be taken- up and dealt with now that we have taken over the Canadian Northern Railway system. It cost about twice as much as that to operate it. There is a big loss.

Some years ago I had a seat in this House when the question of the Transcontinental was very much debated, and there was a good deal of opposition to that part of the line from hon. gentlemen who were, at that time, sitting on the opposition side of the House. Remarks were made in particular to this effect, that the line running through the northern part of the province from Quebec to Cochrane would never prove a paying proposition. Since that line has been built it has opened up a very wealthy part of the province of Quebec, where thousands and thousands of settlers have already established themselves and where immense wealth in the way of pulpwood lies ready for the market. If this line has not brought better results, I think the minister will probably find that the reason is that the equipment is not sufficient to take care of all the traffic coming from that part of the country. The settlers of the Abitibi region have complained over and over again that it is impossible for them to ship their pulp-wood. All along the line from La Reine, Amos, and the different settlements in that district, thousands and thousands of cords of wood are lying, unable to be shipped. If we had had a little more equipment, much more revenue could have been derived from that Toad. The revenue obtained by the road has been obtained without the railway having had an opportunity to meet either of the two purposes for which it was built. These purposes were, first, to decrease the cost of freight on wheat from the West, and secondly, to ensure ocean freight for our Canadian ports. Has this been obtained? I say without the slightest hesitation, no. The figures in regard to exports have not been given by my hon. friend from Quebec county, but I have a few here which I want to place upon Hansard. The exports of grain from Fort William and Port Arthur are as follows:

How is it that the line in question has not been equipped so that the grain of the West could have been shipped through Canadian ports? In my opinion, the Government which came into power in 1911 deliberately conducted matters so as to discredit this line against which they have [DOT]always had a grudge, and they did not take *steps to equip properly this part of the *road, in order that the grain might be diverted to United States ports to the detriment of Canadian ports. Of the ports of Halifax, St. John and Quebec, the one that has most reason to complain is Quebec. We have year after year had promises from different Governments, and every time that the matter seemed to be about to come to a head, a change of Government occurred', and the new Administration immediately upset all the doings of the previous Administration. In 1911, the whole situation in Quebec was very clear and well prepared for the future of the city, when suddenly the Liberal Government went out of power and the new Government that took office afterwards changed the whole situation. We have that instanced especially in the case of the Transcontinental terminals at Quebec. As my hon. friend (Mr. Lavigueur), who is the *mayor of Quebec, stated a few minutes ago, the city of Quebec in 1911 entered into a contract with the Government of Canada by which a beautiful property situated on the St. Lawrence front, a property which was valued at least $2,000,000, was handed over to the Transcontinental Commission for the very modest sum of $100,000, on the condition that the Government would spend in the city of Quebec a sum of not less than $2,000,000 in the way of repair shops and other equipment. The engineers of the Government and the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, which was vitally interested in the *project, had given their consent to all those proposed improvements. They had decided that the shops of the Transcontinental would be on the heights of St. Foy. The

land had already been prepared; a roundhouse had already-been constructed; everything- was settled; when suddenly in 1911 the Liberal Government went out of power *and the Conservatives took office. . At. once the agreement entered into between the city of Quebec and the Transcontinental Commission was thrown aside. The whole project was changed and the shops were diverted from St. Foy to St. Malo, six miles from the main line. I am not complaining about the shops being at St. Malo, although the wisdom of that is disputed, but as they have been built there, the least we can expect from the Government is that the shops shall not remain idle. The shops were erected' two years ago, yet they have no machinery in them yet. I say the shops should be working for the benefit of the Transcontinental Railway. The Prime Minister stated in a speech delivered in the city of Quebec in 1913-at wnich time the present Minister of Railways was in the Cabinet-that the shops would be of benefit to the Transcontinental and the city of Quebec. The only thing that was required to be done, he said, was to build a tunnel from the St. Lawrence water front through the mountain in order to reach the St. Malo shops. In order that there may be no doubt as to what the Prime Minister said at that time, I quote his actual words:
The site originally selected at St. Foy will nevertheless be utilized in the first instance for a large through freight yard which is necessary at that point in order to provide for the distribution of cars on different roads. Moreover, a large handsome station has been completed at St. Foy as well as an eighteen stall engine house and every building necessary for the efficient operation of the railway. Between the Quebec Bridge and the Champlain Market a double track has practically been completed. There is also a connection with the Canadian Northern Railway at Cap Rouge, which permits entrance to the St. Charles side of the city, and which can be utilized for this purpose pending the completion of the tunnel that will connect the St. Lawrence waterfront with the new Ur.ion Station on the Palais site. While that tunnel is essential to the National Transcontinental railway for effective access to the Union Station and to the St. Charles side, it will be equally necessary to other great railway systems which will naturally require access to the great frontage terminal of the St. Lawrence.
The Prime Minister in those words pledged himself to the construction of a tunnel with a view to giving access to the St. Malo shops. I would ask any member who wishes to satisfy himself whether the pledge of the Prime Minister in this respect was carried out, to come to the city of Quebec and see conditions for himself. No CMr. Parent]
tunnel has been built, and I venture to say that no tunnel ever will be built, f would urge the Minister of Railways to take a special interest in that matter, for there is no other city in Canada that would tolerate the situation that exists in Quebec at the present time. The shops are there without machinery and with no work for them to do; it is an intolerable situation. The minister can do what he likes with the shops. If he prefers to hand them over to the Canadian Pacific railway, which was apparently the intention in connection with all railway improvements in the city of Quebec, let him do so, and then we shall not have to complain, because tbe Canadian Pacific railway will use the shops.

Tlhe Dominion Government must, of course, protect any securities that are against the Canadian Northern. As to the general policy of the Government the hon. gentleman cannot expect any announcement from me at the present time. When we sit down to consider the whole situation, questions of this kind will naturally arise, and during the recess we shall have time to consider them, and then at another session we .shall be able to give more information on the whole situation.
I would like,to emphasize this point: When the Government takes over the stock it takes over the whole road and must assume any obligations that are against the Canadian Northern railway, and it will do that. If there are any claims against the Canadian Northern of any kind, they will have to ibe dealt with either by the courts, by negotiation, or by settlement if the accounts are fair and just. I do not think I could add anything to what the Prime Minister has said as to the general railway policy. We want to- get a good board of directors, of able men, and lay the facts before them, and then the questions can be dealt with as they arise.

I regret that the discussions we have on this side of the House seem to be regarded by hon. gentlemen on the other side only with Christian toleration. I see a somewhat amused and contemptuous smile on their -faces whep we talked about the Intercolonial and railway matters in the far East. I want to remind-my hon. friends from Ontario and the West that they have no better customers- in the world than the miners and steel workers of Cape Breton and the lumbermen of Nova Scotia, that their pork, beef, bacon, flour,
farm .implements- and everything they manufacture goes down to these very excellent customers from whom they get their money and to whom they get their products by means of these railways. When we are discussing railways hon. gentlemen from the West and from Ontario must not^ suppose that we are discussing a matter in which they have no concern. We hear uneasy " hear, hears " about passing these items because they do not understand exactly the importance of the subjects that we are discussing. I congratulate the province of New Brunswick upon having a minister who looks after the interests of that province. I hope he will have some success in railway matters. I am sorry that in Nova Scotia it is left to an 'Opposition member like myself to say anything in the interest of that province. We have the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) but he is too busy, of course, to give any attention to such small details as the railway affairs of that province. We have the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. A. K. Maclean) whose world affairs also are of such a character as to remove him from being concerned about such trifling matters as the accommodation of the people in the way of railway facilities. It, therefore, falls inevitably upon such men -as the Opposition members, who have no very great power with the present Government, to get such votes and such considerations as are necessary for railway development in Nova Scotia.
. We are now developing largely as railway owners in our country and the management -and working of railways is a matter that every member should know something about. It is getting to be important. The minister tells us that we have something' like 4,000 miles of road apart from the Canadian Northern railway.
That is right.

It is important for the people that we should have some conception of what we are doing. If this were a meeting of directors it would not he a very cheerful one. The directors, and shareholders would have discovered that we were spending away up in the millions in the development and working of the road but that we have made no money. We are in debt. If we were ordinary directors and shareholders of a road- we would have to put our hands down in our pockets to find money in order to make betterments and to run the road, and that would not be a cheerful prospect. 'However we are new beginners in this enterprise. I was never in favour of

Government ownership; I am not in favour of it now; as I think private enterprise will do better in these matters. Particularly in colonization and development, will private enterprise and private energy do much better than Government ownership. But, by the force of circumstances, we are in this net and we must stay in it and make the most of it that is the way X view it. While a great railway like the Canadian Pacific is being conducted privately we have something to compare our works with. It would be interesting for myself as a citizen of Canada and a member of this House to know how our expenses per mile of operation, for merely running the road, compare with the expenses of the Canadian Pacific. It would be interesting to know how our expenses for betterments, for keeping the road in repair, for rolling stock and all other requirements, compare with those of the Canadian Pacific. Everybody admits that their road is well managed and1 that it is well equipped. It is making money. It is in the same country side by side with ours, and there is no reason why we should not have just as brainy and as capable men to run our road as they have. I would expect the Minister of Railways to come to this House and make a favourable comparison between his railway and the privately owned line and to be able to show that he is making money. There is no reason why the Canadian people should not " make one hand wash the other," or should keep in debt to the extent we are in debt this year. Of course, we are new beginners and we have, to pay for our experience. I do not wish to say anything disagreeable to the minister about the operations of this year. But I must say, in justice to the county and to the part of the province I represent, that we are not treated properly in railway development. We have heard about had railways, poor railways, narrow gauges and roads which are not properly equipped. That is had enough and it is to be hoped that something will be done to better that condition. But I come from an old county, the county in which the famous discoverer landed some three or four hundred- years ago-Cabot is supposed to have landed in Victoria. We have had settlers in that county since then, hut we have never had a mile of railway. My settlers and my people are 100 to 120 miles away from any railway. That is the condition-not a had railway, which is had enough, but no railway at all, which is worse. We thought that in 1911 we had the whole thing in our fist, that we were 
all ready to start building the road: The very first item that the minister mentioned to-night in connection with Nova Scotia reminded me of our old conditions. In 1911, the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government and myself were pulling in the same boat, happy friends. I had my railway and he had his-. I helped- him. He was then in Opposition. He got money for his railway and I got money for mine. The change of Government took place. The Prime Minister went on and built his railway, but he threw me to the wolves-myself and my railway. I do not think that was very fair comradeship or- companionship. I have often chaffed him about it since, but he does- not answer, and there is no answer for it at all. The money was voted for my railroad in the -county of Victoria, jus-t as it has been for the Dartmouth and Dean branch. But I was not prime minister, and the road in Victoria county was not built. The Prime Minister had the power to secure money for a very much poorer section of the country than is to be found in the county of Victoria. I was told at the time by the then Minister of Railways- that something would be done. I moved a resolution in the House that the time had arrived when the non-railway counties in Eastern Canada should be provided with railways. That resolution was accepted, and is to be found embodied in the records. I have been keeping quiet since, but nothing has been done, and, to my surprise and consternation, a couple of years ago six or seven millions of money was invested in a new railway enterprise altogether-in the Quebec and Saguenay railway-and in a new part of the country. What justification was- there to pass over Victoria county, where the enterprise was right in hand, and to undertake a project in a new county as to which nothing had been said about the need of railways at all, and spend this money as it has been spent, more especially in view, of the fact that in the district referred to a railway is not needed half as badly as it is in my constituency? I think I have reason to complain that we have not been properly treated. We have a magnificent country in North Victoria, where there is the finest of fishing, and splendid agricultural land-in fact, everything that is necessary to make of it a great and prosperous district-hut we .have no railway accommodation, although every other part of Canada seems to he getting what it requires for development and receiving proper attention. While I do not hope for very much from anything I say to-night, I

would not be doing my duty to my county if I did not once more impress upon the minister that we have been neglected. The minister remembers well that I am not talking of something which occurred since our party has been in opposition. He remembers well that I kept pounding away at the former Government, of which I was a supporter, until I got them to agree to the building of this railway, and also that I assisted in getting them to agree to build the Guysborough road and the Dean Settlement road. But the present Prime Minister got his own railway built, and1 threw the hon. member for Guysborough and myself, as I said before, to the wolves.
I do not wish to pursue the subject any further, except to say thai, when we from Nova Scotia occupy time in talking about the Intercolonial and railway matters. we have nothing to apologize for. There is one constituent of mine who pays $350,000 to $400,000 to the Government railways.. If the minister will look into thei freight accounts of the Novia Scotia Steel and Coal Company, he will find that one concern pave something like half a million of money into the coffers of this railway, in addition to the large sums paid by other very excellent customers of the railway in that part of the country.
Now, there are a few other local matters that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. Last year I spoke about our station at North Sydney. That is where the Newfoundland traffic is handled, as the minister knows. The trade with Newfoundland during the summer time, when the steamships, on that route are alble to run, is simply enormous. An immense number of passengers travel by that route, and there is a large amount of freight carried, and the money that goes, into the coffers of the Government railway from the terminus at North Sydney must be very large indeed. Unfortunately, the station at North Sydney is a very small one, containing only one small room, and is not at all fit to accommodate the traffic of which I have spoken. I wish to impress upon the minister-and he will remember that I spoke to him last year upon, the same subject-the necessity of providing better accommodation for the public. The existing traffic will amply justify whatever expenditure may be involved in making the accommodation more adequate. The minister will find, if he makes inquiry, that there are no .modern facilities at the station for the needs of the public. The station is but a little bit of a place for a town of the size of North Sydney, and
especially in view of the immense traffic which passes through it. As the member for that constituency, I have often felt ashamed that we did not have better accommodation.
The minister will also recall the fact that I have brought to his attention two or three times the need for better facilities at a place called Molnnes' Harbour. In spite of the poor accommodation the' man in charge has to stay there all the time, and I am sure that if the minister could see the place he would realize that it is not at all suitable. Accommodation for passengers is also lacking, and yet this, is one of the places in the district which pays the road well.
I also, spoke to the minister last year about the need of proper facilities for handling freight at a place called Christmas Island. At that point there is a large amount of freight, but no person to handle it, and no proper station house, and yet the traffic is one that pays well. I sincerely hope that the .minister will give some attention to these matters to which I have drawn his attention. I am talking at a rather unseemly hour, owing to giving way to other hon. gentlemen who had representations to make, but I can assure tlhe minister that I am very much in earnest in urging upon him the imperative necessity of meeting the needs of the people whom I represent. The fact of this being war time compels me to be brief, otherwise I would assure the minister that it would take him three weeks or more to get his. estimates through the House.

The hon. member has acted rightly in bringing these matters to the attention of the committee, because they are now on record, and it will afford me an opportunity of looking into them thoroughly. I want to assure the hon. gentleman that since I have been administering this department I have been, anxious to take the necessary time to make a trip over the Intercolonial railway and look into all such matters as be has spoken of from one end of the road to the other. Perhaps it was hardly fair on my part not to have carried out that intention before, but owing to vPaiiiament being in session, it has so far been an impossibility. However, I have made my plans to take a trip over the Intercolonial, which will include a visit to Sydlney. I wish1 to go to Sydney to see the works, there, and also to visit other parts of Nova Scotia, which, as yet, I have riot had an opportunity of seeing. When I go- bo .Sydney I will discuss matters with

the hon. gentleman and1 come to some conclusion. with respect to some of the things he has mentioned, as well as any other points which need to be dealt with. If there are things that are really necessary, notwithstanding the fact, that this is war time, I will take them up and give them my best consideration. It is only the prevailing war conditions which prevent the Government from doing many things that, we would like to do. However, the hon. member knows the situation as well as l do, and' the difficulties which confront us. Nevertheless I am glad that the hon. member has ventilated these matters this evening, and I repeat that when I am in Sydney I will look into the whole situation. I shall be very glad then to discuss each and every matter that he may bring forward, and endeavour to determine exactly what we should do under the existing conditions.
